issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
Follow-up to #9345. Keep the working isolated CUDA vLLM launcher while making its wheel dependencies and runtime toolchain setup simpler. This is cleanup and validation work, not a known serving failure or a blocker for #9345.

Current state:

- The promoted CUDA 13.2 vLLM wheel requires `torchaudio==2.11.0`. In the verified x86_64 resolution, `torchaudio==2.11.0+cpu` is the only package taken from PyTorch's CPU index. The launcher therefore searches both CUDA and CPU indexes with `unsafe-best-match`; #9345 explicitly requires the CUDA torch build so a conflict cannot silently select CPU torch.
- The launcher installs `nvcc`, CRT, and NVVM at matching versions and creates `lib64`, `libcudart.so`, and `libnvrtc.so` links at startup. Removing the CRT/NVVM pins without validation lets the resolver pair `nvcc==13.0.88` with 13.4.92 compiler components.
- The promoted wheel has H100 and GB200 release validation, and #9345 has H100 serving validation. The final isolated launcher with transitively selected NVRTC has not been specifically exercised through a FlashInfer SM100 JIT path on GB200.

Done when:

1. Check whether the vLLM wheel can express its audio dependency without requiring a second PyTorch index for text serving. Use a single CUDA backend/index if the resulting wheel and supported `uv` version permit it; record an actual x86_64 and aarch64 resolution before removing the current index setup. Remove the explicit CUDA torch version requirement too if the single backend makes CPU fallback impossible.
2. Run a small GB200 FlashInfer SM100 JIT case through the final Marin `IsolatedCudaVllm` launcher, recording the exact wheel, resolved CUDA packages, task image, and job result. Add that coverage to the GPU qualification work in #8800 where appropriate.
3. Remove startup links or compiler-component pins only if the replacement passes the relevant H100 and GB200 checks. Keep a short reason beside each remaining pin or link.

Related: #8800 (future GPU wheel qualification), #7373 (the earlier missing-`nvcc` FlashInfer failure), and draft #9343 (a rollout record that is not intended to merge).

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
Marin accepts `--enforce-eager` through `vllm_extra_args` without explaining its effect. vLLM defaults this setting to false. Enabling it disables both `torch.compile` and CUDA graphs. This can turn a compatibility workaround into a large serving slowdown.

A controlled Snowball A/B used the same September 21 Grug-67B checkpoint, vLLM build, eight-H100 node, DP/EP topology, prompts, and token counts. The only changed argument was `--enforce-eager`.

| Mode | TTFT | TPOT / ITL | Output rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `--enforce-eager` | 245.0 ms | 44.025 ms/token | 22.72 tokens/s |
| vLLM default: compile + CUDA graphs | 83.7 ms | 6.523 ms/token | 153.45 tokens/s |

The default mode reduced per-token latency by 6.75x and TTFT by 2.93x. This closely reproduced the 7.44x decode difference between an older eager playground deployment and current Snowball serving. The [A/B job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fsnowball-enforce-eager-ab-20260922-v2) contains the runtime logs.

The A/B also measured two costs of the default mode. CUDA graphs used about 0.84 GiB per H100, and the default arm spent 25.37 seconds in first-time compilation. Total startup times are not comparable because the eager arm ran first and paid different launch and cache costs. The run did not test failure compatibility, separate compilation from CUDA graphs, or establish output parity. Five of eight greedy output hashes matched; three differed.

Marin's managed vLLM compilation cache was enabled. The compiled A/B identity had no earlier generation and published 1,156 entries: 301 MB before compression and a 35.7 MB archive. The cache uses region-local 30-day temporary storage. We did not run a warm Grug arm, so its cached startup time is unmeasured.

Current `main` enables eager execution twelve times across eleven non-test files. Ten model-catalog YAML files pass `--enforce-eager`. `experiments/post_training/iceball_micro.py` enables it once for SkyRL rollout generation and once for final evaluation. The ten catalog settings came from one imported model-config set. No affected setting records a model-specific reason or validation.

The [vLLM engine arguments](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/engine_args/) document the false default and the disabled optimizations. The [vLLM optimization guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/) recommends eager mode for development or debugging when fast startup matters more than steady-state decode performance.

Done when:

- The shared Marin vLLM launch path emits a warning when the effective arguments enable `--enforce-eager`. The warning states that the flag disables compilation and CUDA graphs and can reduce steady-state throughput. It points to durable documentation or this issue.
- `experiments/evaluation/serve/models/README.md` documents the default, the measured Snowball tradeoff, and when eager mode is appropriate.
- Existing non-test uses are audited. Each use is removed or has a model-specific reason recorded nearby.
- A unit test covers the warning without starting vLLM.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
Apply a checkpoint's `pending_qb_betas` before Grug MoE evaluation callbacks run. A checkpoint-only evaluation at its stop step currently exposes the model parameters and EMA parameters without that pending update. The next normal training forward and the sampling restore path apply the update first, so evaluation can score a different routing state from the one the checkpoint would use on its next forward.

The observed score effect was small on two Hero checkpoints. It was still enough to make the first fixed-policy Paloma comparison semantically incomplete. The original `a1` results are superseded by corrected `a2` runs.

This issue is separate from the router-precision proposal in #8435. The omission occurs regardless of router dot precision. The measured impact comes from checkpoints produced by 20 steps on one B200 rack, so it does not establish the size of the effect for other checkpoints or long runs.

Requested behavior: apply the pending query-bias update to both the current and EMA model views used by evaluation hooks. Ordinary progress, logging, and checkpoint callbacks should continue to use the stored state without launching eager query-bias work.

An experimental fix and regression test exist on Romain's fork, but they have not been merged:

- Initial fix: [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860)
- Final scoped fix: [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40)
- Evaluation wrapper: [`train.py`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L679-L693) and [eval-hook application](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1188-L1195)
- Regression test for current and EMA model views: [`test_eval_callback_models_apply_pending_query_bias`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py#L361-L387)

Done when checkpoint evaluation applies the pending query-bias state to current and EMA models, the regression passes, and non-evaluation callbacks avoid this extra work.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Observed behavior

The checkpoint stores `pending_qb_betas` separately from `params`. The training step applies those betas as centered router bias before the next forward, then stores newly computed betas for the following step. The evaluation callback model getters expose raw `params` and EMA parameters. A forced end-of-run callback at an already reached stop step can therefore evaluate the router bias embedded in the parameters and omit the pending update.

The problem appeared while comparing two step-126020 continuation checkpoints under current router arithmetic. Both checkpoints came from the same complete step-126000 native state:

`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-126000`

[`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83) is the observed production source identity for that checkpoint. It does not identify the experimental continuation code.

The experiment branch was based on [`1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db). The router arithmetic controls used by the experiment were added in [`f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c). The corrected evaluation behavior was introduced in [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860) and scoped to evaluation hooks in [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40).

The two continuations used seed 0, the restored data-loader state, and steps 126000 through 126019:

| Checkpoint | Continuation job | W&B | Checkpoint path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current arithmetic | `/romain/hero-router-current-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/current-a1/step-126020` |
| Preferred FP32 accumulation | `/romain/hero-router-pref-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/preferred-fp32-a1/step-126020` |

### Superseded and corrected evaluations

The `a1` jobs used raw callback model state and are superseded:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22020006 | 0.80684924 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22091150 | 0.80714315 |

The `a2` jobs applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update before the same fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22016478 | 0.80683833 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22088742 | 0.80713451 |

Applying the pending state changed macro loss by `-0.00003528` for the current checkpoint and `-0.00002408` for the preferred-trained checkpoint. The preferred-minus-current macro-loss delta changed from `+0.00071144` to `+0.00072265`. This correction does not change the router investigation's recommendation, but it makes the evaluation represent the complete checkpoint state.

Both corrected jobs completed all 16 tasks without failures or preemptions. Their extracted metrics are at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/fixed-eval-with-pending-qb-a2.json`, SHA-256 `d13af487ee6b7f54644b9dcb5e3d7a37fdcc6e17420b7cf7476652877f8e9182`.

The final investigation report is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/hero-router-training-report.md`, SHA-256 `454aae5894a78c99752cff47301441c9a8d315b30d5d1ddf1410c069bba73f4c`. The review response that prompted and verified the correction is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/goal-review-response.md`, SHA-256 `a5bfff56802f87c14b6be057f4cbd9e6f86d298906071f28cbe77f532217a3d9`.

### Reproduction

Run from the experimental fork at [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40). Set `SOURCE` to either step-126020 checkpoint above. Because `num-steps` equals the restored state step, the optimization loop takes no step and the forced final callback runs Paloma:

```sh
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id <fixed-eval-run-id> \
  --dp-racks 1 --batch-size 1024 --optimizer-batch-size 11264 \
  --gate-router-weight-decay 0.02 --num-steps 126020 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --initialize-from-checkpoint "${SOURCE}" --router-dot-precision current \
  --training-data mixture --eval-every 1 --version dev --run
```

The focused validation command was:

```sh
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 nice -n 10 uv run --frozen --python 3.12 \
  pytest -n 0 --tb=short -q \
  tests/test_grug_hero_scaling_ladder.py tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py
```

Result: 71 passed, with one pre-existing JAX scatter future warning. `./infra/pre-commit.py --changed-files --fix` also passed.

</details>

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
## Description

Marin is starting to run long-lived HTTP services on Iris (e.g. `ducky`, an ad-hoc DuckDB SQL service — `lib/ducky`). Iris has no first-class notion of a "service"/"system" job that stays up best-effort across unlimited preemptions and infra failures, and several defaults are footguns for that use case (all code-verified):

- **Retry budgets are lifetime totals that never reset.** `failure_count` / `preemption_count` on the task only ever increment (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/task.py`); there is no reset for task retry counters anywhere in the controller. Over months of preemptions the budget monotonically climbs to the ceiling and the job goes terminal even if every run lasted days.
- **No "infinite" sentinel.** Enforcement is a plain `count <= max` (`reconcile/task.py:446`, `:208`); `-1` / `0` mean *fewer* retries, so "forever" can only be approximated with a large magic integer.
- **`max_task_failures` defaults to 0 and is a footgun.** It is a job-level cumulative budget: `total_failures > max_task_failures` → `JOB_STATE_FAILED` (`reconcile/job.py:37`). With the default 0, a single hard container failure fails the whole job regardless of `max_retries_failure`. An always-on job that doesn't override it dies on the first OOM/crash.
- **Nothing auto-recreates a terminal/lost job.** No restart policy, no cluster-declared standing-services list the controller reconciles. `existing_job_policy=KEEP` only makes a *client* resubmit idempotent — the controller never resubmits on its own. finelog sidesteps Iris entirely by running as a K8s Deployment with `restartPolicy: Always`.

`ducky` currently works around all of this: an in-process supervisor, `max_retries_{preemption,failure}` and `max_task_failures` all set to `1_000_000`, `existing_job_policy=RECREATE`, and still needs an external watchdog (`ducky deploy --keep` on a schedule) to cover job loss. See `lib/ducky/src/ducky/deploy.py` and `lib/ducky/src/ducky/server.py`.

### Definition of Done

A supported way to declare a long-lived **service job** that:

- retries preemptions/failures effectively forever without per-caller magic numbers — an explicit "unlimited"/restart-policy, or a retry budget that resets after healthy runtime;
- does not die on the first failure by default for the service case (sane `max_task_failures` handling for services);
- is auto-recreated by the cluster if it goes terminal or its state is lost — a declared standing-service list the controller reconciles, or an equivalent — so services don't each need a bespoke external watchdog.

## Related

- #6763 — `IrisDaemon`, the *per-node* (DaemonSet) long-lived-workload primitive. This issue is the *singleton service* (Deployment-equivalent) sibling: one always-on instance, not one-per-node. Both share "a service is a task, inheriting supervision/health/preemption accounting."
- #6722 — service-endpoint leasing (TTL, decoupled from task-row lifetime). Covers the endpoint half of the "survive controller/agent restart" gap noted above.
- #6669 — retry/failure budget field rename. Confirms `max_task_failures` is a job-level cumulative budget changed to *prevent* crash-loop-forever — in direct tension with an always-on service that wants to retry forever. A service primitive should resolve that tension explicitly rather than forcing per-caller `1_000_000` magic numbers.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR (large/design task, no definition of done yet)**

This asks for a *new standalone harness*, not a bug fix. The closest thing today, [`launch_cw_scale.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py), already env-knobs the model shape and stubs the corpus to SlimPajama-6B — but it is wired through the Marin executor, Fray/Iris `ResourceConfig`, and a real tokenize pipeline, so it is neither standalone nor data-free. A truly shareable repro means decoupling the model + train step from all of that and feeding synthetic tokens.

# Research
**Relevant code**
- [`launch_cw_scale.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py) — 90B/256-H100 scale launcher; the perf config to mirror
- [`launch.py#L78-L102`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/launch.py#L78-L102) — `slimpajama_6b_data()`; real tokenize step, the data coupling to cut
- [`train.py#L304`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/train.py#L304) — `train_step`; consumes `GrugLmExample` batches via `DataLoader`/`AsyncDataset`
- [`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py) — `GrugModelConfig` / `Transformer`
- [`grug_moe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py) + [`_moe/ep_deepep.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py) — MoE dispatch / DeepEP GPU expert-parallel backend (the perf-critical path)

Related: #4312 (improve 8×H100 MoE MFU), #6695 (verify CE path in May profile), #6386 (CoreWeave Grug MoE canary scaling).

# Proposed approach (for review before I build it)
A single runnable script (e.g. `experiments/grug/moe/repro_gpu.py`) that:
1. Builds `GrugModelConfig` + the FSDP/expert-parallel mesh exactly as `launch_cw_scale.py` does (reuse `build_scale_model` and the `expert_axis`/`replica_axis` math), but imports **only** Levanter/Haliax/JAX — no `marin.execution`, no Fray/Iris, no executor.
2. Replaces the dataset with an in-process synthetic source yielding random-token `GrugLmExample` batches of the right `[batch, seq]` shape — zero I/O, no tokenize.
3. Runs N steps with the existing `train_step`, warms up past compile, and prints step time / tokens-per-sec / MFU, optionally a `jax_profile` window.

This keeps the perf-critical model + MoE EP code identical to production while removing every dependency an external engineer can't run.

**Decisions I need from you before implementing:**
1. **Target scale** — single 8×H100 node (~9.5B canary class, runs anywhere) or the full 90B/256-GPU multi-node shape? Standalone+shareable argues for single-node by default, multi-node opt-in via env.
2. **"Replicates the GPU performance"** — what's the acceptance metric? Match the real run's step time / MFU within some % at a fixed shape, or just "exercises the same kernels and reports throughput"?
3. **Dependency surface** — strictly Levanter+JAX (so it ships outside this repo), or is "no Marin executor / no Iris, but still inside the marin tree" good enough?

Tell me 1–3 (or just "single-node, throughput-only, inside the tree" and I'll run with it) and I'll open the PR.

comments.body:
🤖 Standalone GPU MoE repro — working, validated on a single 8×H100 node

Added [`experiments/grug/moe/standalone_repro.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/rav/grug-moe-standalone-6759/experiments/grug/moe/standalone_repro.py) on branch [`rav/grug-moe-standalone-6759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav/grug-moe-standalone-6759) (off `main`). Single-file launcher that runs the production grug MoE train step on synthetic data with **no Marin infra** — no iris/fray dispatch, no GCS/R2 data, no W&B required. Just `python -m experiments.grug.moe.standalone_repro`.

**What it does**
- builds the May `d=2560` shape from `main`'s `GrugModelConfig` (fully CLI-configurable: `--hidden-dim/--num-layers/--num-experts/--top-k/--seq-len/--sliding-window/--moe-impl/--attn-impl/--remat`)
- deterministic in-memory token stream (`SyntheticGrugDataset`, ported from the `codex/deepep-*` branch) — zero data I/O, optional periodic EOS + packed `segment_ids`
- builds the compact `(replica_dcn, data, expert, model)` mesh and calls the in-process `_run_grug_local` directly (the same entry each Fray worker runs) — so it needs no dispatch layer
- mesh configurable; **defaults to 2×8×H100** (`--expert-axis 8`, replica = `jax.process_count()`)
- profiling: rank-0 xprof trace logged as a **W&B artifact** under `--wandb`; opt-in `--perfetto-trace` also bundles the perfetto trace (ui.perfetto.dev)

**Validated on 1×8×H100 (`cw-us-east-02a`)** — mirrors the codex single-node `GM2560-…-N1` shape (2 layers / 256 experts):
- run `GM2560-STANDALONE-L2-E8-B8-EOS512-N1-cw-20260701-001025` — finished 30/30 steps, fail=0
- 5.75B params (d2560, 2 layers, 256 experts top-4, seq 4096); E8M1 8-process multi-controller
- loss 1.43 → 1.12; **MFU ~5.5** (p50 5.52); **145K tok/s**; `ring` MoE + `gpu_fa4_cute` + `save_moe`
- xprof trace (steps 8–15) captured on rank 0 and logged as a W&B artifact
- the standalone auto-detected the Iris job context and initialized `jax.distributed` with **no code changes** (same `_run_grug_local` as production)

**Gotchas found running on the iris GPU path** (all worth documenting):
1. `gpu_fa4_cute` requires packed `segment_ids` — run synthetic data with `--eos-interval > 0`; a plain causal mask (`eos_interval=0`) is rejected with `NotImplementedError: … requires packed segment_ids`.
2. iris defaults `JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR` to `s3://…/compilation-cache`, and XLA's per-fusion autotune sub-cache has no `s3://` filesystem driver → `UNIMPLEMENTED: File system scheme 's3'`. Fix: pass a local `JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR` (iris respects an explicit setting). Only bites on the iris path, not an external box.
3. levanter's profiler wrote a perfetto trace on **every** rank and barriered across all ranks — the concurrent perfetto write corrupted/hung (`BadGzipFile`) at 8 ranks. Fixed by adding `create_perfetto_trace` + `profile_process_index` to `ProfilerConfig` (defaults preserve behavior): profile rank 0 only, keep the stop barrier on all ranks. The standalone profiles rank 0 with perfetto off by default.

MFU ~5.5 is expected for this smoke shape (batch 8 = 1/device, only 2 layers → overhead-dominated, `Adam` not `muonh`); scaling layers/batch or switching to muonh raises it. Full `d2560` (26 layers / 256 experts) won't fit one node — it was sized for 32.

Branch is pushed (`rav/grug-moe-standalone-6759`, 3 commits); PR against `main` next.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Summary

Construct the output-path-dependent training config fields in `train_lm`'s `build_config(ctx)` instead of baking them into a blank config later, on the worker, at run time. Retire `bake_output_path` / `_update_config_to_use_out_path` and the separate `output_path` field threading. This is leftover from the old executor framework and is now pure indirection under the lazy `ArtifactStep` model.

## Current shape (config built blank, mutated later, on a different machine)

1. **Coordinator** — `train_lm`'s `build_config(ctx)` (`lib/marin/src/marin/experiment/train.py:131-171`) builds a `TrainLmOnPodConfig` whose inner `TrainLmConfig` has the checkpointer at its *default* base path, `hf_save_path=None`, and `trainer.id` possibly `None`. The real output dir is **not** baked in — it is carried alongside as a separate `output_path=ctx.output_path` field.
2. **Worker** — `run_levanter_train_lm` → `_prepare_training_run` (`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:490-522`) then calls `_update_config_to_use_out_path` → `bake_output_path`, a cascade of `dataclasses.replace` that injects `checkpointer.base_path = <out>/checkpoints`, `temporary_base_path`, and `hf_save_path = <out>/hf`; plus `_enforce_run_id` imputing `trainer.id` from `basename(output_path)`, a cpu `require_accelerator` toggle, and `doublecheck_paths`.

So the config is *constructed* in one place and its path-dependent fields are *filled in* in another, on a different machine, at run time.

## Why it exists (and why it's now obsolete)

The docstring says it outright (`_update_config_to_use_out_path`, `training.py:258`): _"useful when running with the executor framework, where the output path is set by the executor."_ In the **old** executor model, steps were built at **import time**, before the executor assigned the content-hash output path (`name-<hash>`) — the path did not exist at construction, so it had to be baked in late, on the worker, right before launch.

Under the lazy model `build_config(ctx)` runs with `ctx.output_path` already resolved (`{prefix}/{name}/{version}`), so the config can be constructed correctly up front. Verified: `bake_output_path` is a **pure function of `(train_config, output_path)`** with no worker-side dependency — even the region-local temp goes through `marin_temp_bucket(source_prefix=output_path)` (`lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem.py:341`), which derives the region from the **output path**, not the worker VM region. Run-id imputation is just `basename(output_path)`, and the cpu toggle depends only on `resources` — both build-time-knowable.

## Proposed change

- Build the full `TrainerConfig` in `build_config(ctx)` with the real `checkpointer.base_path`, `temporary_base_path`, `hf_save_path` (see #6752 re: dropping the forced HF path), and `trainer.id` — directly from `ctx.output_path`.
- Keep on the worker only what is genuinely run-time:
  - `resolve_training_env` — assembling env vars (GIT_COMMIT, WANDB, JAX compilation-cache dir, accel defaults) and applying them to `os.environ` for levanter;
  - `doublecheck_paths` — the runtime check that configured GCS paths match the live VM region.
- Delete `bake_output_path`, `_update_config_to_use_out_path`, the separate `output_path` field threading, and the run-id-from-output-path imputation; replace "build blank, mutate later" with "build it right once."

## Relationship to #6752

#6752 (HF export as a separate `export_hf` step) wants HF export out of `bake_output_path` anyway. This cleanup naturally removes the forced `hf_save_path` assignment; coordinate the two so the HF path is dropped here and re-introduced as its own step there.

## Blast radius

`_prepare_training_run` is shared by LM **and** DPO (`run_levanter_train_lm` / `run_levanter_train_dpo`) and feeds many experiments; `bake_output_path` / `impute_run_id` are also used by other call sites. This is a real refactor of the shared training entry, not a drop-in — it was not required to make the new steps *run*, only to make them clean.

## Key references

- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:176-200` — `bake_output_path`
- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:249-272` — `_update_config_to_use_out_path` (docstring naming the executor-framework origin at `:258`)
- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:203-246` — `impute_run_id` / `:403` `_enforce_run_id`
- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:490-522` — `_prepare_training_run` (shared LM/DPO)
- `lib/marin/src/marin/experiment/train.py:131-171` — `build_config` that already has `ctx.output_path`
- `lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem.py:341` — `marin_temp_bucket(source_prefix=...)` (region from output path, not VM)

_Filed from the lazy ArtifactStep / executor-context adoption work; surfaced while reviewing the training config path._

# Research

Proposal is **sound and verified**, but this is a refactor of the shared LM/DPO training entry (>100 lines, the issue says so itself), and — critically — **the code it targets does not exist on `main`.** `experiment/train.py`, `build_config(ctx)`, and `ctx.output_path` live only in the branch of #6649 ([`weaver/adopt-executor-context-for-remai`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6649), still OPEN). The issue's line refs match that branch exactly (`build_config` at `train.py:131`, `bake_output_path` at `training.py:176`, `_update_config_to_use_out_path` at `:249`). So this is **stacked-on-#6649 cleanup**, not a `main` change. Per scope rules I'm posting analysis rather than a PR.

Claims I confirmed:
- `bake_output_path` **is** a pure fn of `(train_config, output_path)` — no worker/VM dependency (`training.py:176-200`, branch).
- Region-local temp comes from the **output path**, not the VM: `marin_temp_bucket(source_prefix=...)` — *"An explicit source_prefix fully determines the backend and region"* ([`filesystem.py:378-385`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem.py#L378-L385)).
- Run-id imputation case 4 is `basename(output_path)`; cpu `require_accelerator` toggle depends only on `resources`, which `build_config` already has via `ctx.runtime_arg("train_resources")` (`train.py:168`). Both build-time-knowable. ✔

# Proposed approach (for #6649 author)

The build-time / run-time split the issue describes is correct. **Build-time** (move into `build_config(ctx)`): `bake_output_path` (base_path, temporary_base_path, hf_save_path), run-id, cpu toggle, `_maybe_override_auto_build_caches`. **Run-time, keep on worker**: `resolve_training_env` (GIT_COMMIT/WANDB/JAX cache — its `marin_temp_bucket` call has **no** `source_prefix`, so it's genuinely launcher/region-dependent, `training.py:480-484`) and `doublecheck_paths` (live VM-region check).

Three nuances the "it's just `bake_output_path` + run-id" framing misses — handle these in the move, don't drop them:

1. **Adapter/PEFT path rewrite.** `_update_config_to_use_out_path` also nulls `hf_save_path` and sets `peft_save_path` for adapter LM/DPO (`training.py:265-270`, branch). Pure, so it moves to `build_config` too — but it must move *with* the hf-path logic, and this is exactly the seam #6752 (separate `export_hf` step) wants to cut. Coordinate: drop the forced `hf_save_path` here, reintroduce as its own step there.
2. **Run-id precedence changes.** `impute_run_id` priority is `trainer.id` → `env_vars["RUN_ID"]` → `os.environ["RUN_ID"]` → `basename(output_path)` (`training.py:203-246`). `build_config` already passes `id=run_id` (`train.py:138`), so build-time imputation is usually a no-op — but moving it build-time means a worker-side `RUN_ID` **env var no longer overrides**. Confirm nothing relies on that (Iris/ferry-injected `RUN_ID`).
3. **DPO auto-schedule reads tokenizer stats.** `_maybe_auto_resolve_dpo_schedule` → `_dpo_training_dataset_size` does I/O (`training.py:303-305`). Decide explicitly whether it stays worker-side or moves; it is *not* a pure config transform like the rest.

Net: `_prepare_training_run` shrinks to `resolve_training_env` + `_apply_env_to_process` + `doublecheck_paths`; `bake_output_path` / `_update_config_to_use_out_path` / `_enforce_run_id` / the separate `output_path` field thread get deleted. Land it as a follow-up commit on #6649 (or a PR stacked on it), gated on the #6752 hf-export decision.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Revisited now that the lazy ArtifactStep work (#6649) has landed. Opened #6809 for the cleanup, but with a correction to this issue's proposed mechanism.

**The cleaner way already exists in-tree.** The grug base/moe launchers build their checkpointer paths directly from `output_path` and never touch `bake_output_path`. `train_lm` was the last holdout on the blank-config-then-`dataclasses.replace`-cascade. So the fix is to make `train_lm` match grug and delete the cascade — no new machinery.

**But building the paths inside `build_config(ctx)` (as this issue proposes) is subtly wrong.** `build_config` runs at *fingerprint* time too, with `ctx.output_path == "<output_path>"`. Two consequences the earlier analysis missed:

1. **Region leak into identity.** `temporary_checkpoint_base_path("<output_path>")` → `marin_temp_bucket` can't parse a region from the placeholder, so it falls through to `marin_prefix()` and bakes the *ambient cluster's root* into the fingerprint. Identity would then depend on which cluster you lowered from. (The earlier comment's claim that the temp path is "build-time-knowable and pure" holds for the VM, but not for the fingerprint placeholder.)
2. **Fingerprint churn.** Moving `base_path` into `build_config` changes the fingerprinted value from the default `"checkpoints/"` to `"<output_path>/checkpoints"` — a new hash for every existing train artifact, forcing TPU recompute of cached fixed-version runs.

Grug sidesteps both by keeping path construction in its `run` callable (real `output_path`, after fingerprinting). #6809 does the same for `train_lm`: it deletes `bake_output_path` / `_update_config_to_use_out_path` / `impute_run_id` / `_enforce_run_id` and replaces them with direct construction (`resolve_checkpointer_output_path` + `apply_output_path` + `_resolve_run_id`, the first now shared with grug), while leaving the fingerprint byte-for-byte unchanged.

Scope notes: DPO isn't wired into the lazy layer yet (no `TrainDpoOnPodConfig` constructor in production), so `_prepare_training_run` is shared but only `train_lm` exercised the cascade. The forced `hf_save_path` is preserved for now — dropping it belongs with #6752's separate `export_hf` step, not this structural cleanup.

issues.author: ihodes
issues.body:
A single Python module that is the authoritative source of truth for our chat/response format in BOTH directions: (1) RENDER a conversation → the exact token string the model trains/serves on, and (2) PARSE model output → structured {reasoning / tool_calls / final / tool_results}

Rationale: this is the cheap ~80% of the value of OpenAI’s openai-harmony / Mistral’s mistral-common without adopting a Rust lib or their grammar

# Requirements
- versioned/pinnable
- unit-tested on round-trip (parse(render(x)) == x)
- streaming-aware parse (partial tokens)
- handles the thinking + tool-call + tool-result segments for whatever chat template we pick in Stage 4 (likely Qwen-style)
- framework-independent (usable outside vLLM — in the harness, in notebooks, in eval)

# Design decisions
- do we adopt an existing format’s grammar (Qwen template — richest data) and just own the render+parse for it, or define our own? Either way we own the module. If we ever go channel/Harmony-style (agentic + multimodal pressure), this module is where that complexity lands.

# Needed-by
This is required by the time we need to do thinking mode fusion; we can punt until 2027 worst-case.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description
Track follow-up from #6572 for H100 BF16 fused linear softmax cross entropy at B=32768, H=2560, V=128256. The XLA reference materializes full logits/dlogits (`25.02 GiB` grad module) and measured `32.58ms` forward, `100.10ms` `jax.grad(loss_fn)`, `246,983 tok/s` combined.

The B-tiled custom VJP bounds memory while keeping full-vocab GEMMs. H100 autotune4 timings:

- B tile 2048: forward `34.19ms`, backward `135.08ms`, combined `193,585 tok/s`
- B tile 4096: forward `32.48-34.68ms`, backward `131.26-133.30ms`, combined `195k-200k tok/s`, grad memory `5.05 GiB`
- B tile 8192: forward `35.11ms`, backward `128.09ms`, combined `200,792 tok/s`
- B tile 16384: forward `33.06ms`, backward `122.90ms`, combined `210,107 tok/s`
- Production default 8192 on the clean PR branch: forward `33.73ms`, backward `123.56ms`, combined `208,323 tok/s`

### Definition of Done
- Explain the remaining backward gap against the materialized XLA reference and theoretical GEMM limits.
- Decide whether the production default should stay at 8192 or move with more memory evidence.
- Prototype the next kernel path if it can reduce passes over logits/dlogits without losing the memory win.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis (no PR — research/design task, depends on open PR #6572)**

The B-tile path lives in #6572, not on `main`. This is perf-investigation + a new kernel prototype, all gated on H100 hardware, so per the agent workflow this is an analysis for human review, not a code PR. Code refs below point at #6572's `pallas_gpu.py`.

# 1. Backward gap

The B-tiled backward is ~3 full-vocab GEMMs per tile; XLA `jax.grad` is ~2. The extra GEMM is a logits *recompute* — `_backward_b_tiled_from_lse` saves only LSE in residuals (the memory win), so it re-runs `x_block @ w` before computing dlogits, then does the two grad GEMMs (`dlogits @ wᵀ`, `xᵀ @ dlogits`).

Roofline at B=32768, H=2560, V=128256, bf16 — one GEMM = 2·B·H·V ≈ **21.5 TFLOP**:
- Forward (1 GEMM): observed ~33 ms → ~650 TFLOP/s ≈ 66% of H100 dense bf16 peak. GEMM-bound, near roofline; matches XLA forward (32.58 ms) as expected — same single GEMM either way.
- B-tiled backward (3 GEMMs = 64.5 TFLOP): ideal ~99 ms at fwd efficiency; observed 123 ms (default 8192) → ~525 TFLOP/s.
- XLA grad (2 GEMMs, logits already materialized): 100.10 ms, but pays 25.02 GiB HBM round-trips on logits/dlogits.

So the ~23 ms backward gap (123 vs 100 ms) ≈ the recompute GEMM. It is **not** inefficiency — it is the recompute-vs-materialize trade the memory bound buys. The path is already GEMM-bound; you can't close the gap without either storing logits (defeats the memory win) or removing the HBM round-trips of logits/dlogits via fusion (item 3).

**Relevant code (in #6572)**
- `_backward_b_tiled_from_lse` — recompute `x_block @ w`, then dlogits + 2 grad GEMMs per B-tile.
- `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_full_vocab_b_tiled` — forward, materializes one `[b_tile, V]` per tile.
- `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` — H100/bf16/B≥8192/V≥65536 policy gate, returns `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_BLOCK_SIZE = 8192`.

# 2. Production default: keep 8192

The reported B-tile sweep (193k → 210k tok/s from 2048 → 16384) is a tiling-overhead curve: bigger tiles → fewer `fori_loop` iters, larger GEMMs, better MXU utilization. But peak transient memory scales linearly with the tile — per-tile `[b_tile, V]` f32 logits + dlogits:
- 4096 ≈ 4.2 GiB (+ ~1.3 GiB f32 `grad_w` accumulator) → matches the reported 5.05 GiB.
- 8192 ≈ ~10 GiB; 16384 ≈ ~20 GiB.

16384 buys ~1% over 8192 (210k vs 208k tok/s) for ~2× peak logits memory, eroding most of the headroom under the 25 GiB XLA reference and squeezing co-resident activations. **Recommend the default stays 8192** unless a real memory budget shows ≥10 GiB free headroom at the target shape; revisit only with that evidence.

# 3. Next kernel path

The win is removing the logits/dlogits HBM round-trips, not removing a GEMM. The current B-tiled backward materializes full `[b_tile, V]` logits **and** dlogits to HBM (~8 GiB each at 16384). A fused Pallas kernel — B-tiled **and** V-streamed, FlashAttention-style — would keep each `[b_tile, v_block]` logit/dlogit tile in SRAM, fuse the recompute GEMM + softmax + dlogits + both grad accumulations, and never write the logit volume to HBM. That pushes backward from ~525 toward the ~650 TFLOP/s the forward already hits (~99 ms target), keeping the memory bound.

Template already in-tree: the forward `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_pallas_gpu_fa_style_streaming` and the V-streaming `_backward_streaming_from_lse` (used on the non-H100 path). The prototype is a backward analog that nests V-streaming inside the B-tile so both dims stay tiled in SRAM. Note the current forward/backward route through the materializing XLA reference because "JAX 0.10 Mosaic GPU does not lower the tiled pallas_call dot_general path" — so this path is blocked on Mosaic GPU lowering support and should be prototyped against that constraint.

Next steps for a human: (a) confirm the recompute-pass attribution with an H100 profile of the backward (expect ~1 GEMM-time of `x@w` recompute), (b) prototype the fused B-tiled+V-streamed backward once Mosaic GPU lowering lands, (c) re-sweep memory headroom before moving the 8192 default.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
🤖

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment investigates why Grug MoE MuonH is much slower than the same single-node H100 recipe without Muon: May140 MuonH5 ran at 1.492s/step and 21,962.5 tokens/s, while May141 SGD reached about 0.438s/step and 74,848 tokens/s. The work tried grouped/stacked Newton-Schulz implementations for expert matrices, including bounded chunking, padded stack sharding, a 4D grouped layout, and a standalone optimizer-update harness. The main result so far is negative for simple grouping: unbounded grouping OOMed during autotune, bounded grouped/padded MuonH did not improve full training throughput, and harness runs show the isolated NS/dot kernels are already reasonably efficient. The best remaining direction is not another full train profile; first make the production optimizer consume data-sharded grouped NS results without restore/all-gather boundaries, or evaluate algorithmic reductions such as fewer Newton-Schulz steps or fewer Muon-treated matrices.

### Helpful links
- May141 SGD A/B isolating roughly 1.05s/step of Muon/update overhead: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6493#issuecomment-4738899640
- May143 bounded grouped/padded MuonH full-run result with no throughput gain: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6493#issuecomment-4739656808
- H1/H3/H5 layout comparison and current recommendation: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6493#issuecomment-4741396380
- Latest padded/sharding harness note on why restore/all-gather boundaries erase the distribution win: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6493#issuecomment-4741473425
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Single-node CoreWeave H100 profiles show Grug MoE MuonH/Newton-Schulz dominates the May d2560 B8 step. May140 MuonH5 ran at 4.7499 MFU, 21,962.5 tokens/s, and 1.492s/step. The May141 SGD A/B on the same single-node shape reached 16.09 MFU, 74,398 tokens/s, and 0.440s/step at first metrics. The profile suggests many Muon/Newton-Schulz GEMMs are emitted as separate GPU kernels instead of grouped work.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Make Muon fast enough for the single-node Grug MoE path by grouping compatible matrices into stacked/batched Newton-Schulz tensors, sharding the stack axis over `expert`, and unpacking/resharding updates back to parameter layout. XLA flag sweeps are secondary; the main goal is to express larger batched work.

### Links

* Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-muon-gpu.md`
* May140 MuonH5 baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-140S4096-W2048-B8-R1-E8M1-XLACE-RING-REPEMB-REPOUT-FA4MUON5-SCOPED-PROFILE-N1-cw-20260618-0623
* May141 SGD A/B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-141S4096-W2048-B8-R1-E8M1-XLACE-RING-REPEMB-REPOUT-FA4SGD-AUTOTUNE-PROFILE-N1-cw-20260618-0637

## Results

TL;DR: exploratory evidence says Muon costs roughly 1s/step on the single-node B8 profile.

Scope: single-node first, `model_axis=1`, no TP/multinode experiments, outputs under `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d`.

Current baseline: May140 MuonH5 B8 profile at 1.492s/step versus May141 SGD at 0.440s/step.

Decision log:
- 2026-06-18: prioritize grouped/stacked Muon implementation over additional TP or broad compiler flag work.

Negative results index:
- May136/May137 no-autotune and no-reshard variants stayed slow; disabling autotune was a major confound.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Status:** Analysis only — this is a perf/design experiment (multi-module, well over 100 LOC, no single bug + definition-of-done), so no PR per agent policy. Root cause + proposed approach below for human review.

# Research

The May140 "MuonH5" path runs Newton-Schulz **one matrix at a time**, vmapped over the scan/stack axis, and column-shards each matrix over `("data","model")`. It never groups matrices into a batched/stacked NS tensor, so each expert (and each layer) emits its own GEMM trio per iteration — the kernel explosion the profile shows. The exact optimization this issue proposes is already written down as a TODO in the NS helper, and is already implemented (for 3D expert params) in the `grug_muon` config — but not on the MuonH path the slow run uses.

**Relevant code**
- [`util.py#L244`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/util.py#L244) — `zeropower_via_newtonschulz5`, per-matrix NS used by MuonH
- [`util.py#L275-L283`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/util.py#L275-L283) — TODO proposing exactly this (shard per-layer / stack similar layers); current shard is `P(None,("data","model"))`
- [`muonh.py#L164-L176`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/muonh.py#L164-L176) — MuonH applies NS via `map_flattened_linear_layers` (vmaps scan layers, no stacking)
- [`grugmuon.py#L311-L346`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L311-L346) — `_zeropower_via_newtonschulz_batched_stack_sharded`: batched NS, stack axis sharded
- [`grugmuon.py#L45-L64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L45-L64) — `_batch_sharded_stack_target_pspec`: shards stack axis over all mesh axes with size>1, else falls back to vmap

# Proposed approach

Three options, cheapest first:

1. **A/B the existing `grug_muon` config on the single-node B8 shape** before writing any new code. `grug_muon` already defaults to `STACK_BATCH_SHARDED` ([grugmuon.py#L152](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L152), [#L219](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L219)) and batches the 3D expert weights (`w_up_gate`/`w_gate_up`/`w_down`) with the expert/stack axis sharded. This directly tests the hypothesis with zero new implementation. The `VMAP_REPLICATED` layout is the natural A/B baseline.

2. **Single-node caveat to check first.** With `model_axis=1`, `_batch_sharded_stack_target_pspec` shards the stack(expert) axis over every mesh axis of size>1 and requires `num_experts % total_shards == 0` ([grugmuon.py#L59](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L59)). For E8 on 8 devices that divides, but any param whose leading stack dim isn't divisible silently falls back to plain `vmap` ([grugmuon.py#L208-L217](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/grugmuon.py#L208-L217)) — i.e. back to the slow path. Confirm via profile that the batched-stack branch is actually taken; if it falls back, that fallback (not Muon math) is the real cost.

3. **If MuonH math is required** (constant-norm projected update, [muonh.py#L179-L192](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/muonh.py#L179-L192)), port the batched-stack NS into the MuonH path rather than re-deriving it: stack same-shaped matrices into a leading batch axis, run `_zeropower_via_newtonschulz_batched_stack_sharded`, unstack. The genuinely new work beyond `grug_muon` is **cross-layer/cross-matrix stacking of the 2D (non-expert) matrices**, which no path does today — that is the larger design piece and should be scoped only if step 1 shows expert batching alone doesn't close the gap to SGD's 0.440s/step.

Notes: the referenced logbook `.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-muon-gpu.md` does not exist in the repo. Related: #6404, #5613, #6388 (MuonH NS ablations), PR #6118 (HybridMuon), #3445 (MoE perf roll-up). Recommend starting with option 1 (a config swap, no code) and reporting the profile before implementing 2/3.

| H1 dot-only | ~10.29 ms | ~5.15 ms | 0 | expression forms tied |
| H5 pure NS4D | 58.2477 ms | 29.1239 ms | 0 | ~5.35 PF/s, ~67.6% of 8xH100 dense bf16 peak |
| H5 dot-only | ~50.84 ms | ~25.42 ms | 0 | ~6.12 PF/s, ~77.4% of 8xH100 dense bf16 peak |

Harness correction: the initial speed-of-light percentage denominator was one H100; it now divides by device count (`devices * 989 TF/s` nominal dense bf16 H100 peak). Local `py_compile` passes on the current harness. The main-thread validation also passed `uv run pytest lib/levanter/tests/test_grugmuon.py experiments/grug/moe/test_optimizer.py -q` after that patch.

I also launched a redundant H5-only confirmation before seeing the primary-result update: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260618-101451`, output `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L2-H5-DOTONLY-N1-cw-20260618-1016-4507ea`. It agrees directionally: pure NS4D 61.90 ms / 2 layers, dot-only about 54.34 ms / 2 layers, no compiled collectives.

Conclusion: `einsum`, `jnp.matmul`, and explicit `lax.dot_general` tie for these raw 4D NS dot shapes. The isolated dot kernels are already roughly 70-77% of nominal dense peak, so this no longer looks like a bad expression-form/XLA-lowering problem. The Muon train-step gap is mostly real algorithmic GEMM volume. Next work should move up a level: fewer NS steps, distributing the NS work across data/replica nodes, or reducing which matrices receive Muon.

Change:

- The padded variants take an original unpadded group, use input sharding `P(None, expert, None, None)`, pad the group axis, reshard compute to `P(data|replica_dcn, expert, None, None)`, run NS/dot-only, restore group-axis replication, then slice back.

Local smoke command:

```bash
XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=8 uv run python experiments/grug/moe/muon_update_bench.py \
  --layers 2 \
  --ns4d-group-size 3 \

  --max-grouped-stack-size 512 \
  --replica-axis 1 \
  --data-axis 2 \
  --expert-axis 4 \
  --model-axis 1 \
  --ns4d-group-axis data \
  --orthogonalization-layout stack_batch_4d_sharded \
  --bench-kinds ns4d_data_group,ns4d_padded_group,ns4d_dotonly_matmul_padded \
  --mode both \
  --disable-abstract-mesh \
  --warmup 1 \
  --iters 1 \
  --output /tmp/muon_bench_padded_smoke.json
```

Smoke result:

- Unpadded `ns4d_data_group` correctly skips when group size 3 is not divisible by `data_axis=2`.
- Padded variants report input `P(None, 'expert', None, None)`, compute `P('data', 'expert', None, None)`, padded group size 4, H1 6 two-batch-axis dots.

This is useful signal for production design: padding is feasible for measurement, but the slice/restore boundary can erase the distribution win unless the optimizer can consume the padded/sharded result directly.

comments.body:
🤖 Muon path handoff for the next owner, status as of 2026-06-18 15:05 PDT.

## Current conclusion

The Muon-only single-node target is now met in the standalone update harness, but the production training path is not yet proven fixed.

Best current gate:

```bash
MUON_BENCH_PROFILE=fullprod-e8-l26-h3 \
bash scratch/muon_update_bench_fast_loop.sh iris
```

Run:

- Parent: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260618-153021`
- Output: `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-E8-FULLPRODMUONH-G4-H3-N1-cw-20260618-153016-87deb1`
- Shape: one 8xH100 node, d2560, L26, `expert_axis=8`, `data_axis=1`, `model_axis=1`, `ns4d_group_size=4`, H3, bf16.

Results:

| bench | H3 time / 26 layers | peak fraction | compiled AG/AR/RS |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| routed expert grouped MuonH | 0.5236 s | 58.63% | 0/0/0 |
| full production MuonH | 0.6171 s | 50.56% | 0/0/0 |

Interpretation: the full-shape production H3 update-only path clears the requested ~50% Muon speed-of-light gate. H5 also clears the target in the lean update-only harness at 54.28%, but H3 is the practical production-speed compromise because it is ~1.55x faster than H5 on L26.

## What is proven

- Single-node E8 grouped/full-production MuonH3 can run as a standalone optimizer update with zero compiled all-gather/all-reduce/reduce-scatter.
- The fast loop is now first-class:
  - `experiments/grug/moe/muon_update_bench.py`
  - `experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_muon_update_bench.py`
  - `scratch/muon_update_bench_fast_loop.sh`
  - `experiments/grug/moe/MUON_UPDATE_BENCH.md`
- The harness reports wall time, estimated NS FLOPs, effective TFLOP/s, peak fraction, matrix counts, group estimates, sharding specs, stack chunks, and lowered/compiled collective counts.
- D2/E4 pure grouped NS/apply can also be collective-free if the grouped representation is preserved through apply.

## What is not proven

- The current full train optimizer path has not been shown to consume the grouped production representation without reintroducing restore/split boundaries or scheduling overhead.
- The H3 full training profile is still slow: May153 H3 B8 train was 6.437 MFU, 29,763 tokens/s, 1.1009 s/step, with xprof assigning about 55.6% of device self-time to `optimizer_muon`.
- D2/E4 should not be used for a full train run until the production optimizer can keep grouped params/updates/results as `P(data, expert, None, None)` through apply. The old restore/split path inserts all-gathers.

## Important negative results

- May140 MuonH5 single-node full train: 4.7499 MFU, 21,962.5 tokens/s, 1.492 s/step.
- May141 SGD A/B same basic B8 shape: 16.1876 MFU, 74,848.2 tokens/s, 0.4378 s/step. This isolated roughly 1 s/step of Muon/update overhead.
- May142 unbounded grouped Muon OOMed during autotune on `bf16[832,2560,2560]`.
- May143 bounded grouped/padded MuonH5 succeeded but did not improve full-train throughput: 4.6705 MFU, 21,595.4 tokens/s, 1.5174 s.
- D2/E4 restore-boundary harness showed pure `P(data, expert, None, None)` NS is healthy, but restoring/splitting back to per-layer leaves inserts 18 compiled all-gathers and erases much of the distribution win.

## Recommended next steps

1. Do not launch another unchanged full May train profile from Muon work.
2. Use `MUON_BENCH_PROFILE=fullprod-e8-l26-h3 bash scratch/muon_update_bench_fast_loop.sh iris` as the fast gate for optimizer changes.
3. Wire the grouped/full-production H3 representation into the production optimizer path, or add a narrow train/apply integration gate that proves:
   - grouped expert params/updates/results preserve the intended `NamedSharding.spec`,
   - compiled AG/AR/RS remain `0/0/0` in the optimizer/apply boundary,
   - no restore/split all-gather boundary appears before `optax.apply_updates`.
4. Only after that gate passes, launch a full single-node H3 train profile and compare against:
   - May153 H3: 6.437 MFU / 1.1009 s.
   - May141 SGD: 16.1876 MFU / 0.4378 s.
5. For scaling beyond one node, test 32 GPUs then 128 GPUs with `model_axis=1`. The axis to validate is whether Muon overhead drops when the grouped stack can shard over more non-model axes without introducing gradient/application collectives.

- Handoff/status file: `scratch/profiles/single_node_grug_moe_status_20260618.md`
- Muon update harness runbook: `experiments/grug/moe/MUON_UPDATE_BENCH.md`

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on trying to make the grouped→FSDP restore boundary coarser.

I added `expert_fsdp_grouped_target_restore_boundary` in `6144c5d99`. Instead of restoring the 4D grouped update to `P(None, expert, None, None)` and then constraining each split leaf to the FSDP param layout, this variant first reshards each grouped 4D tensor directly to a 4D FSDP-compatible layout:

- `w_gate_up`: `P(None, expert, data, model)`
- `w_down`: `P(None, expert, model, data)`

Then it splits into ordinary per-layer FSDP leaves.

Run:

- Iris parent: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-073428`
- Run id: `MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D2E8-TARGETRESTORE-G4-H3-N4-cw-20260619-0734`
- Summary path: `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D2E8-TARGETRESTORE-G4-H3-N4-cw-20260619-0734-599cd3/summary.json`
- Same R2/D2/E8, L26, G4, H3 setup as the previous attribution run.

Results:

| bench | mean seconds | compiled AG | compiled A2A |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `expert_fsdp_grouped_restore_boundary` | 0.3042 | 150 | 0 |
| `expert_fsdp_grouped_target_restore_boundary` | 0.3086 | 112 | 0 |

So the target-layout restore reduces the compiled all-gather count but does not improve time; it regresses slightly. The logs also emit repeated XLA SPMD warnings for the target-layout variant:

`Involuntary full rematerialization. The compiler cannot go from sharding {devices=[4,1,1,1]<=[4]} to ... efficiently ... As the last resort, SPMD will replicate the tensor and then partition it to obtain the target sharding`.

This rules out the simple “reshard the whole 4D group directly to FSDP layout before splitting” fix. Combined with the prior attribution, the restore boundary remains the problem: XLA is not giving us an efficient grouped→FSDP redistribution for this representation. The likely next path is not another placement tweak inside the same restore; it is either a grouped/model-consumable expert parameter representation, or an explicit custom/coarse redistribution path that avoids relying on SPMD to synthesize many grouped-to-FSDP reshards.

🤖 Grouped-parameter target result: this is the speed target if the model can consume grouped expert params directly.

I ran the existing grouped-param optimizer/apply path against the FSDP restore+apply path on the same R2/D2/E8, L26, G4, H3 setup.

- Iris parent: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-073920`
- Run id: `MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D2E8-GROUPEDPARAMTARGET-G4-H3-N4-cw-20260619-0739`

Results, using task 0 summary row:

| bench | mean seconds | compiled AG | compiled A2A | mean H100 bf16 peak % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `expert_grouped_muonh_optimizer_apply` | 0.1612 | 0 | 0 | 47.62 |
| `expert_fsdp_grouped_updates_muonh_apply` | 0.4058 | 150 | 140 | 20.37 |

Interpretation: grouped expert params are the viable fast target. The update+apply math itself can run at ~48% nominal H100 bf16 peak with no compiled collectives when params and updates stay grouped. The FSDP-master + grouped-updates + restore-to-FSDP-before-apply path is ~2.5x slower because of the conversion boundary, not because MuonH compute is slow.

This strongly suggests the implementation path should change from "optimizer-only grouped updates restored into ordinary FSDP leaves" to "expert weights have a grouped/model-consumable representation". The Levanter `MoEExpertMlp` forward currently expects rank-3 per-layer expert weights (`[E, D, I2]` and `[E, I, D]`), so making grouped params real is a model/storage change: either expose per-layer views from grouped expert banks, or move expert banks out of per-layer `Block` leaves and have block calls index the appropriate group/layer.

Run `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-081308`; summary prefix `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D2E8-FP32NS-BF16-G4-H3-N4-APPLYONLY-cw-20260619-081306-7a1457`. comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update on the grouped-to-FSDP boundary path:

I added an explicit `shard_map` restore-boundary probe on branch `codex/research-grug-moe-d2560-mfu` at `7fe217504`. The probe converts grouped expert updates back to FSDP update leaves by explicitly all-gathering only over the grouped layer axis (`replica_dcn,data`) and then slicing the matrix axis by `data`, instead of relying on XLA to infer the reshard.

What we learned:

- The explicit boundary fixes the bad reshard lowering shape. Full L26 lowering on R2/D2/E8 showed semantic HLO `all_gather=14`, `all_reduce=0`, `reduce_scatter=0`, `all_to_all=0`, `dot_general=0`, with no replicate-then-partition warnings observed before runtime.
- Full L26 fp32 restore-only still OOMs when returning the whole restored update tree. Both `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-085051/...EXPLICITRESTORE-G4-N4...` and `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-085526/...EXPLICITRESTORE-NOPARAM-G4-N4...` failed with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` on a 32.81 GiB allocation at `block_until_ready_tree(next_updates)`. Removing the unused synthetic FSDP params did not solve this; the output update tree itself is the memory cliff.
- A bounded L8 fp32 timing probe succeeded: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-090020/...L8-R2D2E8-EXPLICITRESTORE-G4-N4...`. It compiled to 32 all-gathers, 0 AR/RS/A2A/dots, and ran at about 0.17436s.
- Full L26 bf16 restore-only succeeded: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-090318/...L26-R2D2E8-EXPLICITRESTORE-BF16-G4-N4...`. It compiled to 112 all-gathers, 0 AR/RS/A2A/dots, and ran at about 0.3055s.

Interpretation: explicit `shard_map` is a useful primitive because it prevents XLA GPU from silently choosing the replicate-then-partition path. But returning a complete per-layer fp32 FSDP update tree is still not a production path. Even when it fits in bf16, the full restore-only boundary is about 0.305s, so the next credible implementation needs to either fuse/stream explicit restore into apply, returning only next params, or avoid the per-layer FSDP update-tree boundary by keeping grouped expert-bank params model-consumable.

I recorded the details in `.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-muon-gpu.md`.

| May194 | N4 B64 R2/D2/E8, auto stack over replica_dcn=2,data=2 | Succeeded. Steady final: mfu=6.8043, mean_mfu=4.7972, tokens/s=125,846.3, duration=2.0830s. |

May194 confirmed the intended mesh in W&B: `replica_dcn=2`, `data=2`, `expert=8`, `model=1`, `batch_shards=32`. It ran to `JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED` with all 4 tasks succeeded. The shutdown coordination warnings were after W&B finish and terminal success.

Interpretation:

- The production path now works end-to-end across single-node, 2-node R2, and 4-node R2D2 without the original 36 GiB OOM.
- It is not yet performance-successful. May194 regresses badly versus May193: more nodes increased tokens/s only from ~102.9k to ~125.8k, while step duration worsened from ~1.27s to ~2.08s and MFU fell from ~11.1 to ~6.8.
- That points at a production integration/communication boundary problem, not just Newton-Schulz math throughput. The next useful work is HLO/profile inspection of the grouped-to-FSDP conversion and apply boundary, plus checking whether the live full-shape grouped stack is actually preserving shardability over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)` rather than inducing expensive per-leaf collectives.

bf16 Newton-Schulz note:

- Current grouped path default `ns_compute_dtype="input"` means bf16 updates run NS in bf16, but fp32-param/update runs do fp32 NS unless `--muon-ns-compute-dtype bf16` is set.
- Local deterministic probe from the worker: fp32 input, bf16 NS vs fp32 NS had cosine ~0.99831 and relative RMS ~0.0192 on small expert-like grouped shapes. That is promising for update-only speed tests, not a train-quality proof.
- Existing update-only benchmark notes already show fp32-input R2/D2/E8 bf16 NS about 1.9x faster than fp32 NS. The new production knob lets us test that in the full train path.

Suggested next run after profiling/HLO sanity:

```bash
experiments/grug/moe/run_cw_may_d2560.sh \
  --expert-3d-optimizer grouped_muonh \
  --muon-ns-compute-dtype bf16
```

I would not keep scaling this exact production path until we understand why R2D2 slowed down so much relative to R2.

Real optimizer, bf16 params/state diagnostic:

- StableHLO: `AG/AR/A2A/RS=2/0/0/0`.

- The real optimizer path with bf16 params is in the same broad runtime range (~0.55s) but compiles to more A2A (`42`) and still has low realized peak.

Separate bf16-vs-fp32 NS check from Lorentz:
- Successful N1 d2560 L2/L4 probes show bf16 NS is about 1.86x-1.97x faster than fp32 NS.

- child `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-155146/grug-train-MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D2E8-REALGROUPEDMUONH-UPDATEONLY-FP32-CAP256-H3-N4-cw-20260619-155144`

- Failed before timing.

- Runtime OOM: allocation `27.34 GiB`.

- `optax.apply_updates` is not the primary fp32 memory trigger. Removing it reduced the failed allocation from ~28.71 GiB to ~27.34 GiB, but the graph still has the same ~79.69 GiB peak.

- `replica_axis=2`, `data_axis=2`, `expert_axis=8`, `model_axis=1`, `layers=26`
- `dtype=float32`, `ns_compute_dtype=bf16`, `nesterov=false`, `backend_steps=3`, `ns4d_group_size=4`
- Metadata compute sharding: `P(('replica_dcn', 'data'), 'expert', None, None)`
- Lowered HLO: `all_gather=14`, `all_reduce=0`, `all_to_all=0`, `reduce_scatter=0`, `dot_general=126`

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: added a sequential grouped-bank consumer gate to close the realism gap in the grouped-bank result.

Change:
- Added `expert_grouped_sequential_bank_consumer` to the Muon update harness.
- It consumes persistent grouped expert banks one layer at a time from rank-3 expert-local activations, instead of feeding all layers in a group independently as `[group, expert, tokens, hidden]`.

Result:
- Unsharded group-axis smoke works: `dot_general=8`, `AG/A2A/AR/RS=0/0/0/0` for a 4-layer tiny case.
- Target sharded group axis (`ns4d_group_axis=replica_dcn,data`) is now a structured skip before lowering. The original direct attempt fails with JAX `ShardingTypeError`: a single layer slice from a 4-way sharded group axis has output size 1, which is not divisible by the mesh axis.

Interpretation:
- This is the caveat on the fast grouped-bank gate. Keeping grouped params/updates/results is fast, but a conventional sequential block loop cannot just index `GroupedMoEExpertMlp.layer()` from a `replica_dcn,data`-sharded group. That access pattern needs an explicit communication boundary, a lower-level custom one-layer access path, or a grouped/scan-like model consumer that keeps the group axis alive.
- So the all-at-once grouped-bank consumer remains a useful lower bound, not proof that the ordinary transformer loop can consume a grouped bank directly.

Validation:
- `uv run pytest experiments/grug/moe/test_muon_update_bench.py -q` -> 52 passed
- `./infra/pre-commit.py --changed-files --fix` -> OK

Next:
- Do not port grouped banks into the real model by calling `GroupedMoEExpertMlp.layer()` on a sharded group axis. The next design should either keep the group axis through a grouped/scan consumer or make the one-layer access boundary explicit and measure/overlap it.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 R2D1 grouped-MuonH bridge decomposition finished and points pretty clearly at the representation boundary, not `optax.apply_updates`.

Run:
- Parent: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-231730`
- Child: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-231730/grug-train-MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D1E8-GROUPEDMUONH-DECOMP-H3-G2-CAP512-N2-cw-20260619-231728`
- Output: `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D1E8-GROUPEDMUONH-DECOMP-H3-G2-CAP512-N2-cw-20260619-231728-b9110a`

Exact May198/May202 mesh: 2 nodes, `replica_dcn=2`, `data=1`, `expert=8`, `model=1`, L26/d2560, 256 experts, grouped MuonH3, group size 2, cap512, bf16 NS.

Key results:

| bench | compiled AG/A2A/AR/RS/CP | median | mean | note |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| real grouped MuonH update | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.496s | ~0.496s | full optimizer update path |
| real grouped MuonH apply | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.477s | ~0.478s | update + restore/apply path |
| grouped-updates MuonH update | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.302s | ~0.303s | starts with updates already grouped |
| grouped-updates MuonH apply | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.307s | ~0.308s | grouped updates -> MuonH -> restore -> apply |
| explicit slice-first gather restore boundary | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.223s | ~0.223s | restore only |
| explicit slice-first gather restore+apply boundary | 26/0/0/0/0 | ~0.229s | ~0.228s | restore + ordinary apply |

Interpretation:
- The bridge is no longer exploding into A2As; the compiled shape is 26 all-gathers and zero A2A/AR/RS/CP.
- Ordinary `optax.apply_updates` is not the bottleneck. Restore+apply is only about 5ms slower than restore-only.
- The outbound grouped-to-FSDP restore boundary is about 0.22s by itself.
- The inbound FSDP/unreduced-gradient/momentum -> grouped layout tax is roughly `0.496s - 0.303s ~= 0.19s`.
- May198 grouped MuonH full train vs May202 SGD control had about a 0.40s/step Muon tax, which is almost exactly explained by inbound grouping plus outbound restore.

So the next useful work is reducing/avoiding/hiding the grouped<->FSDP representation boundary. Optimizing normal `apply_updates` is not the lever. The two plausible directions are: keep grouped expert banks/updates live longer so the model or optimizer consumes them directly, or replace the slice-first gather bridge with a lower-level/custom grouped-to-FSDP permutation that avoids or overlaps these 26 expensive all-gathers.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: direct target-FSDP reshard was not enough on XLA GPU.

I tested the proposed grouped-to-target-FSDP bridge on R2D1/E8/L26:

- Parent Iris job: `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260619-235217`
- Output: `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D1E8-TARGETFSDP-H0-CAP512-N2-cw-20260619-235215-c54af4`
- Config: 2 H100 nodes, `replica_dcn=2`, `data=1`, `expert=8`, `model=1`, group axis `replica_dcn,data`, group size 2, cap 512, bf16 params/updates, bf16 NS compute, MuonH3.

Result:

| bench | lowered AG/A2A/AR/RS/CP | compiled AG/A2A/AR/RS/CP | median |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| target-FSDP chunked restore+apply | 0/0/0/0/0 | 26/0/0/0/0 | 0.2384s |
| explicit slice-first gather restore+apply | 26/0/0/0/0 | 26/0/0/0/0 | 0.2282s |

Interpretation: the obvious `reshard(..., P(None, 'expert', 'data', None))` path looks clean before GPU compilation, but compiled HLO reintroduces the same 26 per-layer all-gathers. It is also slightly slower than the explicit slice-first gather baseline on this bench. So this rules out plain target-layout resharding as the pragmatic grouped-to-FSDP bridge.

Next direction: either keep the expert bank persistently grouped across the model/optimizer boundary, or implement a manual grouped-to-FSDP conversion (`shard_map` first, then Pallas/Triton if needed) so XLA cannot rewrite it into 26 independent all-gathers.

🤖 Update: packed slice-first grouped-to-FSDP bridge was tested and rejected.

- Change: Added a harness-only `expert_fsdp_grouped_packed_slice_first_gather_apply_boundary` bench. It packs all grouped updates for one expert weight name before restoring to FSDP leaves, trying to reduce the outbound boundary from one all-gather per layer/group to one larger all-gather per expert weight name.
- Run: parent `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260620-000715`, child `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260620-000715/grug-train-MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D1E8-PACKEDSLICEFIRST-H0-CAP512-N2-cw-20260620-000713`, output `s3://marin-na/tmp/ttl=7d/experiments/grug-moe-cw/muon-update-bench/MUON-BENCH-D2560-L26-R2D1E8-PACKEDSLICEFIRST-H0-CAP512-N2-cw-20260620-000713-67247f`.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: grouped-trace MuonH profile and apply-memory diagnosis

- Change: Added profile capture/reporting to the Muon update harness and measured the current best R2D1E8 L26 grouped-trace update path.
- Result: update-only `real_expert_fsdp_grouped_muonh_optimizer_update` succeeds at ~0.302s on 2 nodes / 16 H100s, about 50% nominal H100 bf16 peak for estimated NS dot work. Compiled HLO still has 26 all-gathers and 572 GEMM custom calls.
- Profile evidence: the profile is communication-heavy. Per local GPU there are 26 NCCL all-gathers totaling ~252-269ms, plus 234 NVJet GEMMs totaling ~180ms. The all-gathers are bandwidth-scale, not tiny latency-only ops: byte estimates for this shape are ~130.9GB global expert update tree, ~8.18GB grouped input/device, and ~16.36GB FSDP output/device, or roughly 600MiB/GPU per AG if spread evenly over 26 AGs.
- Negative result: donating params+grads+state still OOMed on the full ordinary apply path with a 16.41GiB allocation, matching the per-device FSDP expert output tree size.
- Diagnostic result: `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc_async`, and `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.98` made the full apply path fit, but runtime collapsed to 2.05-2.78s, so this is diagnostic only, not a performance path.
- Interpretation: NS compute is no longer the first-order problem in the harness. The remaining blocker is the grouped-to-FSDP restore/apply boundary. JAX-level direct reshard/packed variants have already compiled into the same 26 AGs or worse A2A patterns, so the next useful lane is a lower-level grouped-to-FSDP bridge or a persistent grouped expert-bank representation.
- Local artifacts on the working branch: `scratch/muon_update_profile_phase_table_20260620.md`, `scratch/profiles/muon_update_profile_20260620_022411_report.md`, and `scratch/best_grouped_muonh_reference.py`.

🤖 Update: H100 direct restore-and-apply comparison

I ran the compile-only G8/R2 H100 comparison for three paths: restore then `optax.apply_updates`, direct restore-and-apply at the FSDP leaf, and persistent grouped params/apply. Parent Iris job `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260620-045028` succeeded.

Both FSDP restore/apply variants lowered with zero collectives but compiled to `AG/A2A/AR/RS/CP=8/0/0/0/0`; persistent grouped compiled to `0/0/0/0/0`. Direct apply compiled faster (`~2.1-2.7s` vs `~7.3-7.5s`) but it is not the grouped-to-FSDP fix.

Interpretation: this falsifies leaf-local direct `apply_updates` as the production bridge unless a future runtime profile shows a separate memory/overlap benefit. The remaining viable paths are (1) explicit coarse transport/custom-call/FFI/Axolotl-style routing for grouped-to-FSDP, or (2) persistent grouped expert-bank ownership with an explicit sync boundary to model-consumable layout.

The detailed table is now in `.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-muon-gpu.md` on branch `codex/research-grug-moe-d2560-mfu`.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: FSDP-master grouped MuonH objective audit

I added a requirement-by-requirement audit for the conservative objective: keep expert train-state/master params in FSDP layout, compute MuonH in grouped NS-friendly layout, convert grouped updates back to FSDP before ordinary `optax.apply_updates`, and avoid the per-leaf collective explosion.

Current status:
- FSDP params at the harness boundary: partial/covered by `real_expert_fsdp_grouped_muonh_optimizer_*` and grouped-trace benches.
- Grouped MuonH compute: achieved in the harness, with grouped-update/grouped-trace paths around the expected speed-of-light band.
- Semantic conversion back to FSDP before apply: achieved by several harness variants.
- Avoiding the compiled collective explosion: not achieved. Direct target-layout reshard, tuple-returning `shard_map`, custom partitioning, packed bridges, ppermute bridges, and grouped-trace restore/apply all still compile into grouped-to-FSDP all-gathers or worse A2A/CP patterns on H100.
- End-to-end performance proof for the FSDP-master bridge: incomplete.

Interpretation: the remaining blocker is specifically the compiled grouped-to-FSDP bridge. The next FSDP-master attempt needs to be a lower-level/custom transport that beats the explicit slice-first baseline; another JAX-level `reshard` wrapper is unlikely to satisfy the objective. The grouped-bank model-consumer path remains the best zero-boundary alternative, but that is a representation pivot until the model consumes grouped banks directly.

🤖 Retargeting this issue around the conservative FSDP-boundary proof.

Current goal is not just "make grouped Muon fast". Grouped Muon compute is plausibly fast in isolation. The missing proof is the expert-weight boundary path:

1. `fsdp_grads_to_grouped_chunks`: normal FSDP gradient leaves -> NS-friendly grouped chunks sharded over `replica_dcn`, `data`, and `expert` where possible.
2. `grouped_updates_to_fsdp_apply`: grouped Muon updates -> either an FSDP-shaped update tree before ordinary `optax.apply_updates`, or direct application into FSDP params.

Immediate pass/fail criteria: correctness vs a simple reference, peak HBM, collective count/bytes by type, wall time, effective GB/s, and compiled-HLO fragmentation. Expert weights first; per-block VJP train-loop work is explicitly future work.

Lowered HLO remains misleading; compiled HLO plus timing is the gate. Route B remains the best current apply-side semantic baseline, and the next FSDP-master work should be lower-level/custom transport or a different layout rather than another wrapper around the same packed restore.

All seven N1/R1D2/R1D4 Iris parents succeeded. The important new result is R1D4/FSDP-data, where `data_axis=4`, `expert_axis=8`, `model_axis=1`, group size 8:

| Primitive | Mean seconds | Compiled collectives | Estimated global bytes | Per-device grouped/FSDP | Effective global GB/s |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FSDP grads -> packed grouped bank | ~0.08136-0.08138s | AG/AR/RS/A2A=`0/0/0/2` | 121.875 GiB | 3.80859375 GiB | ~1608 |
| packed grouped updates -> FSDP update tree -> `optax.apply_updates` | ~0.08417-0.08421s | AG/AR/RS/A2A=`0/0/0/2` | 121.875 GiB | 3.80859375 GiB | ~1554 |

This preserves the thing we needed: no compiled all-gather/all-reduce/reduce-scatter, and exactly two all-to-alls per logical packed boundary. Compared with R1D2, R1D4 halves the per-device payload from 7.6171875 GiB to 3.80859375 GiB and roughly halves the wall time from ~0.172-0.185s to ~0.081-0.085s.

Route A remains at least as good as Route B, so I still do not see a reason to bypass `optax.apply_updates` for speed. The pragmatic integration path is grouped-bank transport back to an FSDP update tree, then normal apply.

Caveat: full-size correctness is still skipped by the harness because the estimated global expert update is 130862284800 bytes, above the current 1 GiB correctness cap. The small-shape tests cover the primitive lowering/correctness path, but we still need an explicit reduced-size distributed correctness run if we want a non-skipped device-side correctness row.
