comments.body:
🤖 Audit of the eleven-rack evidence as of September 9, 22:21 UTC: the NCCL 2.30.7 header build is a promising mitigation, but the record does not support treating all four clean windows as tests of that change. My subjective confidence that the header update materially reduces or resolves the specific ragged-A2A hang is about 60%; this is an engineering judgment, not a statistical posterior or a claim that the failure is eliminated.

Installation logs and distinct process-zero `train_loss` steps give this corrected inventory. Counts include the completed step carrying the restored step number; the earlier comments reported slightly smaller counts at their observation cutoffs.

| Eleven-rack run | PJRT build | Compiled NCCL headers | Completed step records | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| September 3, `ra2a-8870-w1-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 165: 54000–54164 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w2-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 72: 54000–54071 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w3-hero11` | `3091aa7302d8` | 2.30.7 | 185: 54000–54184 | No recorded hang; instrumented wheel |
| September 9, production attempt `72aad6e7` | `b183c591142c` | 2.30.7 | 217: 81716–81932 | Still progressing at the cutoff |

All four used NCCL runtime 2.30.7. The verified newer-header exposure is therefore 402 completed steps across two runs; 237 additional clean steps used the old headers. The earlier statement that every clean reproduction used newer headers was incorrect. The [first two windows](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5534213125) also omitted the checkpointer's per-step broadcast. The [third window](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5547757908) restored that broadcast but added bounded barriers, wait instrumentation, initialization waits and post-collective device-to-host copies. Its success cannot isolate the header change.

Today's run is stronger evidence. It has 176 running tasks, 704 GPU processes, PJRT `b183c591142c`, NCCL runtime 2.30.7 and QuACK 0.6.4. The wheel's source change from production's `3a8f3392723e` is the two-line NCCL build-default update in [XLA PR #22](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/pull/22). The live `train.py` hash matches main, and the batch-ready host barrier is absent. The preceding production attempt `1515615f` used PJRT `3a8f3392723e` with NCCL 2.29.7 headers and runtime 2.30.7; it completed 43 steps from the same restored step 81716 before stalling. Today’s wheel omits the September 4 diagnostic barrier timeouts and device-to-host wait-record copies. This is useful evidence against those diagnostic copies or the proposed host barrier being necessary for the current improvement. It is still one uninstrumented success, with build toolchain, allocation and timing differences, rather than a randomized wheel A/B or a tested restart sequence. Old-header clean windows and the [September 5 pooled-wave run’s contained NVLink error](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) keep alternatives credible; that separate failure shows hardware can also cause a similar stall.

There is also preliminary numerical and performance evidence. Comparing today’s run with `1515615f` over matched steps 81726–81758, loss differed by at most 0.000110 nats, with mean treatment-minus-control +0.0000076. The mean of the reported `throughput_mean_mfu` samples was 21.626% for the new wheel versus 22.110% for the earlier attempt, a decrease of 0.484 percentage points (2.19% relative). These 33 matched steps are observational and do not establish a performance regression or non-regression. Sustained training and restart validation remain open.

For reproducibility, the historical execution IDs are `iris:227df97f1c61d78c`, `iris:8a8e59dcdce56776` and `iris:153389937ce684a7`; today's control and treatment are `iris:a8d3026cb58a0341` and `iris:aa61bafbfdef1160`. Counts use `levanter.metrics`, `name='train_loss'`, `process_index=0`, deduplicated by execution and step. The Marin hub lagged today's regional metrics: 196 records through 22:13:27 UTC on the hub, with the remaining 21 through 22:21:17 UTC verified on `cw-us-east-08a`. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) and [wheel-pin PR #9062](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9062) track the current mitigation.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The source audit found two concrete deadlocks in the remote GIN branch, but neither explains the measured `gin=false` hero path. Zero-size updates skip completion signals that the receiver still counts. Separately, receiver CTA0 can snapshot a shared signal after another CTA's current-launch sends arrive, then wait for an unreachable count. Both predate [3a8f3392723e](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/3a8f3392723e321d806012c5aab492a73bd194c3); these are independently checked protocol schedules, not GPU reproductions.

No missing local CTA synchronization was found in the executed LSA branch: NCCL already joins CTA threads before release publication, and kernel completion joins the matching peer-copy barriers. That result depends on valid metadata, matching grids, serialized barrier resources and CTA progress. It does not locate the original blocked operation. A preceding GEMM or stalled peer-memory transaction can strand peers at the next ragged barrier; the earlier finite-copy-loop argument does not exclude either.

Fresh Finelog analysis confirms larger checkpoint-adjacent dips. Across 1,567 intervals between successive completed-step timestamps per arm (each labeled by its ending step), ragged had eleven intervals above 1.5× its 17.598-second median, all within checkpoint state step through step+4; pooled-wave had one above 1.5× its 19.610-second median. Same-day old-header attempts hung after 43, 0, 0 and 0 completed steps; the new-header trial ran about 300 steps before cancellation and the release hung after roughly 1,590. The upstream review found no change to the device-copy/barrier implementation from fork base `dcf304bc5d` through main `5718ca7411` (September 10, 17:11:56 UTC). [52a0596243](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/52a05962435a168467cc9f8443d3f83a14cbe2af), which explicitly prevents a deadlock, only changes one-shot debug bounds checking, outside the selected device path. comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Offline decode of the [September 15 missing-peer dump](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/441) narrows the stall to a self-deadlocked CTA inside QuACK 0.6.4's SM100 grouped GEMM, and identifies the one code path that separates the warps that retired from the warps that did not. QuACK is not exonerated: the rank stops inside this kernel with no external dependency left, and the deadlock is structural to its CLC scheduler. The initiating condition is still unproved, and two reproduction attempts at production shape did not trigger it.

The stuck kernel is the `dh` backward GEMM (`quack_grouped_gemm(dy, w2, cu, b_major="k")`, tile 256x256, cluster 2x2x1, CLC on). Both resident clusters show the same state in every CTA: the MMA warp and all four epilogue warps have exited, the TMA load warp waits on an A/B empty barrier that the exited MMA warp will never release, and the scheduler warp is still inside its CLC loop. The scheduler ring holds three valid grants (work indices 3996/4032/4068 in one cluster, 4011/4047/4083 in the other), and the ring's barrier words show every warp released grants 1-4 while only the four scheduler warps released grant 5. So the MMA and epilogue warps decoded grant 4 as "no more work" and retired, while the load and scheduler warps decoded the same grant as a valid batch-1 tile and kept going. The load warp's registers hold the batch-1 window `[2214, 4182)` (369 and 328 M-clusters for the first two groups), inside which index 4032 is valid; the retired warps must have used a window ending in `(4011, 4032]`. No invalid CLC response was ever in the ring, so this is not the spurious-cancel failure fixed in 0.6.4.

Every warp role decodes its own tile from `cu_seqlens` in global memory (`VarlenMTileScheduler._delinearize_work_idx`, with a per-warp cached batch window). Only the load and scheduler warps execute `griddepcontrol.wait` first (SASS `ACQBULK` at kernel offsets +2272 and +10528); the MMA and epilogue warps' `cu_seqlens` loads (+15408, +21696) come before any wait, and upstream main still has the same placement (`336a5ca` "Enable PDL"). The kernel is launched with PDL (`use_pdl=True` default) and the XLA fusion after it was already resident at its `ACQBULK`, so the sequence is PDL-chained. Under the hero's `save_moe` remat, `cu` is recomputed in the backward by a small fusion, so a predecessor that writes `cu` is plausible. That is the only per-role difference in the decode path and the natural explanation for a role-consistent split, but a one-time stale read at kernel start does not by itself produce the observed state: the retired warps rescan the window at later grants, and a fresh rescan resynchronizes them. The observed state requires those warps to keep seeing stale group boundaries for the whole kernel, which I could not reproduce.

Two probes on `cw-us-east-08a` (2 nodes, production priority, both clean, `/mwittmann/8870-quack-pdl-repro-2` and `/mwittmann/8870-quack-moe-bwd-probe-1`): (1) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_pdl_repro.py`, the production `dh` GEMM at 601,088 rows with the routing alternating every launch so a stale decode is visibly wrong, six arms (production config, PDL off, CLC off, QuACK patched to wait in the MMA/epilogue warps, constant routing, and the `cu` writer as the immediate predecessor), 600 launches per GPU per arm on 8 GPUs, 28,800 launches, zero hangs and zero output mismatches; (2) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_moe_bwd_probe.py`, the full `_expert_mlp_quack_wgrad` forward plus backward with a fresh random routing every iteration, 1,500 iterations per GPU on 8 GPUs, 72,000 GEMM launches, zero hangs, zero non-finite values. The hero rate is roughly one hang per 1e6 GPU-steps, about 3e-9 per GEMM launch, so a clean 1e5 launches neither confirms nor excludes the PDL path. In probe (1) the PDL-off arm ran at the same speed as production (27 ms versus 27 ms per launch), so disabling PDL on these launchers costs nothing measurable at this shape.

What this changes: the pooled-wave backend runs dense einsums and never touches this kernel, which matches its clean record. CLC off alone removes the per-grant decode (the scheduler warp decodes once and broadcasts) but leaves the initial-tile decode per warp, so it converts most of this failure into wrong or missing tiles rather than a hang, at the 5-12% GEMM cost recorded in `sonic_cute.py`. The cheap, targeted mitigation for the next hero restart is `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers (or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, arm `patched`, to propose upstream); its efficacy can only be judged by the hang recurrence interval, currently one to two thousand steps.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Decoding the step-108711 dump (`/tmp/8870-watch-108711/`, task 90) the same way as the step-107501 one adds two facts that the earlier dump could not give, because this one has seven stuck clusters instead of two.

Six of the seven clusters split at a shared threshold. Their scheduler rings hold grants 4305-4404, the load and scheduler warps hold the fresh windows (group 1 is work indices `[2220, 4398)`, group 2 is `[4398, 6558)`; both are in the load warps' `R7/R8/R9` and the scheduler warps' `R8/R9`), and the ring barrier counts show which grant the MMA and epilogue warps retired on: 4358, 4363, 4365, 4340, 4362, 4367 after accepting 4324, 4328, 4332, 4305, 4327, 4333. The retired warps' end of work therefore sits in `(4333, 4340]` in all six clusters, one value, 58-64 indices short of the real end of group 1. That is one stale set of group boundaries shared by 24 CTAs on 24 SMs, not per-CTA noise.

The seventh cluster (blocks 12-13, initial work index 6) is stuck on its very first tile. Its load warp holds the fresh group-0 window `[0, 2220)` and has filled six A/B stages of tile 6 that were never consumed (A/B full parity 1, empty parity 0 in every stage), its scheduler ring holds one grant (index 13, released by the four scheduler warps only), and its MMA and epilogue warps are gone. The MMA warp exited before issuing a single MMA, so it decoded the initial tile, `idx 6 < 2220`, as no work. That is a decode from `cu_seqlens` that says the kernel has fewer than seven clusters of work, taken in the first microseconds of the kernel, by exactly the warps that do not execute `griddepcontrol.wait`. This case needs no persistence argument at all, which was the gap in the previous comment: a stale read at kernel start deadlocks the CTA on its first tile directly. The six other clusters show the same read at a slightly later moment, with `cu_seqlens[1]` already current and the later boundaries not, which fits a buffer being written while the non-waiting warps read it.

One correction to the earlier reading of the scheduler warps: they are parked at the CLC throttle `bar.sync` (kernel offset +11968) waiting for a load-warp credit that never comes, and the reported PC is the following `TRYWAIT`. With that, every barrier count in both dumps reconciles (loads on the tile the MMA warp abandoned, scheduler one credit ahead).

Taken together with the SASS (only the load and scheduler warps wait before their first `cu_seqlens` load), I now put the PDL-stale-input mechanism well above the alternatives. The `cu_seqlens` read the monitoring agent added to the capture is the confirming measurement: on the next hang, the buffer should hold the boundaries the load warp used (`[0, 2220)` and `[2220, 4398)` in work-index units are 370 and 363 M-clusters of 256 rows) while the retired warps evidently used a set that ended around 723 clusters in total. Independently of that read, `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers, or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, is the change to trial at the next relaunch.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla
spillover_issues.body:
CPU jobs with `--reserve H100` should use available H100 capacity to select among eligible federation peers. This matters for CPU coordinators that later launch GPU child jobs. Iris hands the whole job tree to one peer, so the children cannot select another cluster with more capacity.

After #9356, five successive CPU jobs with `--reserve H100` all completed on `cw-rno2a`. Each requested 0.1 CPU, 1 GB memory, 1 GB disk, and no GPU. The two H100 peers were reachable and advertised the necessary attributes. A report after the tests showed 7 free H100s at RNO and 160 at `cw-us-east-02a`. This report does not establish capacity at each placement decision. A control job without `--reserve` completed locally on `marin`.

Live evidence: [reservation job 1](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Freserve-h100-9356-repeat-20260924-b1), [reservation job 5](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Freserve-h100-9356-repeat-20260924-b5), and [local control](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fno-reserve-9356-control-20260924-b).

CPU jobs have [no numeric accelerator-capacity requirement](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L364-L395). Thus, free GPU counts do not affect their placement score. The [peer-name comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/availability.py#L313-L321) then selects `cw-rno2a` when the other scores are equal.

Done when:

- CPU jobs with `--reserve H100` prefer eligible peers with more available H100 capacity when other constraints are equal.
- Successive and concurrent submissions distribute across peers with equal eligibility and capacity scores. One unchanged availability report must not cause every submission to select the same peer.
- The reservation remains a hard eligibility constraint. Capacity influences placement preference without GPU allocation or a capacity guarantee for later child jobs.
- Explicit cluster pins and local placement without `--reserve` retain their current behavior.
- The policy defines behavior for stale or missing availability reports and for zero free GPUs at every eligible peer.
- Tests demonstrate these cases, and the federation documentation explains the policy.

Related: #9354, #9356, and #7099.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

`--reserve H100` emits an `availability:h100` EXISTS marker, which [survives routing filtering](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L1041-L1046) and gates eligibility. The numeric side is separate: [`peer_availability_gate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L386-L398) reads the job's `DeviceConfig`, so a CPU job produces an empty gate and [`build_queued_candidates`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/federation_store.py#L66-L78) stores no capacity signal. Every eligible peer then scores `(shape_only=False, preempts=False, remaining=0.0)` in [`_place_on_peer`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/availability.py#L376-L399), and the [`peer.peer_id` tie-break](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/68f0ea20785fc86e976741111f5d9ad53c236cf5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/availability.py#L313-L321) selects `cw-rno2a` for every submission.

Peers do supply the number. A single-GPU-variant Kubernetes backend reports `availability.amounts[<variant>]` keyed by the same lowercase variant string the marker carries, so `available:h100` is readable for exactly the peers `availability:h100` admits.

**Proposed Fix**

Carry the marker variants as a preference, not a gate. `QueuedCandidate` gains `preferred_tokens`, built from the `availability:<variant>` markers minus tokens the hard gate already counts. `_Placement` gains a `headroom` term after `remaining`, ranking a backend by the negated effective capacity of those tokens, so more free H100 sorts first. Nothing is spent and nothing is reserved for a preferred token: eligibility and allocation are unchanged.

For the spread requirement, the `peer_id` tie-break becomes a per-job rendezvous key (`blake2b(job_id, peer_id)`) with `peer_id` kept as a stable final fallback. Equal-scoring peers then split by job id instead of collecting on the alphabetically first peer, and the pass stays pure and deterministic.

Degenerate reports fall out of the ordering rather than needing a rule: a backend with no metric already sorts last under `shape_only`, a metric backend that reports no amount for the token counts 0, and zero free everywhere ties at 0 and spreads. The job is still placed in all three cases.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Draft PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9399

`QueuedCandidate` carries `preferred_tokens` — the `availability:<variant>` marker variants the hard gate does not already count — and `_Placement` ranks them after best fit by the same effective capacity the gate reads. The token is never spent, reserved, or required, so the reservation stays hard eligibility and the later GPU children get no capacity guarantee. The `peer_id` tie-break became a per-job rendezvous hash, so equal-scoring peers split across submissions.

Against the done-when list: a metric-less backend still sorts behind every backend the parent can measure, a backend reporting no amount for the token counts as zero, and zero free everywhere ties at zero and still places the job. Pins and local placement are untouched — a pin confines the job before placement runs, and a locally feasible job never enters the queue.

Tests cover the capacity preference, the spread, zero-free placement, reading capacity a GPU job took earlier in the same pass, and the no-double-count rule for a token the job also requests, plus one end-to-end handoff through `promote_queued_federation`. All four behavioral cases fail with only the ranking removed. `lib/iris/tests/cluster` is green at 2340 passed; the four `test_cuda_staging.py` failures there reproduce on the merge base.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Actionable as a design proposal, not a PR.** This is a new CI-triggered deploy capability touching production infra with real trigger/safety design choices (which services, what triggers a redeploy, rollback), so posting analysis + proposed approach for review rather than a unilateral PR.

# Research

Both services already have mature deploy CLIs; what's missing is a CI job that runs them after a build/test passes. There's already a working precedent for CI-driven deploys with GCP auth.

- **finelog** deploys to a GCE VM running `ghcr.io/marin-community/finelog:latest`; restart re-pulls the image. Safe path with health-check + rollback exists.
- **ducky** is an always-on Iris TPU job; redeploy is an idempotent `--keep` watchdog submit that needs a controller tunnel.
- CI already does this pattern for the Iris controller (GCP SA auth, ephemeral OS Login SSH, run the CLI), triggered by cron + manual — no `workflow_run`-on-success deploy exists anywhere.

**Relevant code**
- [`iris-dev-restart.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/iris-dev-restart.yaml) — existing CI deploy pattern to copy (SA auth + OS Login + CLI restart)
- [`finelog/scripts/safe_deploy.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/scripts/safe_deploy.py) — `rollout`/`rollback` with health check; digest cached for rollback
- [`finelog/deploy/_gcp.py#L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_gcp.py#L189) — `gcp_restart()` (`finelog deploy restart marin`)
- [`ducky/deploy.py#L67`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/ducky/src/ducky/deploy.py#L67) — `submit_ducky()`; `ducky deploy --cluster marin --keep`, auto-tunnels, region-pinned TPU job
- [`ops-docker-images.yaml#L100-L109`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-docker-images.yaml#L100) — builds/pushes `finelog:latest` (weekly + dispatch); the natural upstream to gate finelog redeploy

# Proposed approach (design)

Add one deploy workflow per service, cloning the `iris-dev-restart.yaml` scaffold (checkout → `google-github-actions/auth` with `IRIS_CI_GCP_SA_KEY` → ephemeral OS Login SSH → run CLI → remove key). As services multiply, factor the auth+OS-Login boilerplate into a composite action under `.github/actions/` so each new service is ~15 lines. Both start with `workflow_dispatch` so they can be exercised manually before any auto-trigger is armed.

**finelog** — trigger via `workflow_run` on **Ops - Docker Images** completing successfully (that's what publishes `:latest`; restarting on merges that don't rebuild the image is pointless). Deploy step uses `safe_deploy.py rollout marin`, not raw `deploy restart`, so a bad image auto-rolls-back on health-check failure. This is genuinely small and low-risk.

**ducky** — heavier: needs a controller tunnel and submits a TPU job, and `--keep` is a no-op when the job is already healthy (only picks up new code on job restart). Suggest a separate, later workflow (or scheduled `--keep` watchdog) gated on `Ducky - Unit` success on `main`; worth its own discussion before wiring.

**Open questions for reviewers:**
1. Trigger model — `workflow_run` on the upstream build/test, or `push: branches:[main]` with `paths:` scoped to the service dir? I lean `workflow_run` so we only deploy artifacts CI actually validated.
2. Redeploy cadence — event-driven per merge, or keep it a daily scheduled refresh like `iris-dev-restart`? Per-merge finelog restarts are cheap; per-merge ducky TPU-job churn may not be desirable.
3. Should finelog redeploy always go through `safe_deploy.py` (rollback) — I assume yes.

If the trigger model + safety story above is agreed, I'll open the finelog workflow first (small, self-contained) and follow with ducky separately. cc @rjpower

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Depth scaling at fixed width (d512)** — does adding layers + data track the width scaling law, where does the per-layer gradient go with depth, and can we lift the starved early-layer experts.

### Initiating prompts (user)
> lets take the d512 baseline moe, and run it again with 12, 18, and 24 layers. Scale data volume by 2x, 3x, 4x.

> lets take our 4 fasttrack-moe baselines, and plot out the grad at the midpoint in training as a function of layer depth ... I want to see if early layers have a smaller grad

> follow agent.md and make an issue for depth scaling ... [+ depth-study per-layer grads, attn-gate norm per run, attn-residuals + loss comparison]

> lets try the idea from [alltoall notion, "save lower-layer moe experts"] ... apply an auxiliary loss to the output of the first layer for the first 1k steps ... aux loss 0.1 at init, decay linear to 0 over 1k steps ... another version 3k steps. Run both for all 4 sizes of the d512 [depth] ladder.

### Setup
- fast_track MoE, `hero-bpe-v16384` (vocab 16384), SEQ_LEN 4096, 8×H100 (1 node), data-matched, project `marin-community/marin_moe`.
- **Depth ladder** — d512 at 6/12/18/24 layers, token budget 1×/2×/3×/4× (`--num-layers` × `--data-mult`). **Width ladder** — `fasttrack-moe-{d512..d1280}`.
- Metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss` (final).

## 1. Depth scaling vs the width scaling law
![depth vs width scaling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/depth_vs_width_scaling.png)

Width fit `L = 1.2 + 58.97·C^(−0.0843)` (matches README `1.2 + 58.67·C^(−0.0842)`). The d512 depth ladder lands on the width compute-efficiency frontier, with a small penalty growing to +0.014 macro loss by L24.

| ladder | config | layers | FLOPs | Paloma | vs law |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| depth | d512 1× | 6 | 3.46e17 | 3.156 | −0.002 |
| depth | d512 2× | 12 | 1.23e18 | 2.963 | +0.004 |
| depth | d512 3× | 18 | 2.69e18 | 2.860 | +0.013 |
| depth | d512 4× | 24 | 4.65e18 | 2.787 | +0.014 |
| width | d768 | 8 | 2.28e18 | 2.872 | — |
| width | d1024 | 12 | 1.41e19 | 2.633 | — |
| width | d1280 | 14 | 4.26e19 | 2.504 | — |

## 2. Per-layer gradient magnitude over depth
Width baselines: ![grad by depth — width](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/grad_norm_by_depth.png)
Depth study: ![grad by depth — depth](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/depth_grad_norm_by_layer.png)

Routed experts monotone-increasing with depth (smallest at layer 0); shared flat + final spike; attention mid-hump then collapses at the deepest layer. Consistent across width and depth. (Caveat: routed experts train under Muon + load-balancing, so small grad-norm ≠ undertrained by itself.)

Attention-gate param norm by layer: ![attn gate norm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_gate_param_norm.png) — deeper models push the early-layer attention gate harder.

## 3. Kimi Attention Residuals (exploratory)
Reverses the deep-layer attention-grad collapse (attn grad stays high/peaks at depth): ![AttnRes attn grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_attention_grad.png)
Full redistribution (std solid vs AttnRes dashed, matched midpoint step): ![AttnRes grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_grad_by_depth.png)
Loss (all final): AttnRes beats standard at every depth — L12 2.953 vs 2.963, L18 2.855 vs 2.860, **L24 2.775 vs 2.787** (−0.005 to −0.012); small but consistent (parked). ![AttnRes loss](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_loss_comparison.png)

## 4. First-layer auxiliary loss ("save lower-layer experts")
Read block 0's output through the shared LM head, add a next-token CE weighted **0.1 → 0 linearly over 1k or 3k steps**. Run on the d512 depth ladder (6/12/18/24). Question: does early supervision leave the first layer with durably higher gradient, and does it help loss?

**Layer-0 gradient over training** (L6 washes out — too short; L12 persists after decay): ![aux layer0 grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_layer0_grad.png)

**Routed experts specifically — the effect is large and lasting** (layer-0 routed grad, normally the smallest in the net, stays multiples above plain after decay): ![aux layer0 routed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_layer0_routed_grad.png)

| post-decay (5k→end) | plain | aux1k | aux3k |
|---|---|---|---|
| L18 | 0.0027 | 0.0077 (2.9×) | 0.0135 (5.0×) |
| L24 | 0.0015 | 0.0051 (3.4×) | 0.0103 (6.9×) |

**Routed grad, full profile by layer** — the boost is localized to the first ~2–4 layers, flattening the starved early end; deep layers unchanged: ![aux routed profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_routed_grad_profile.png)

**Attention-gate norm by layer** — the supervised first layer shifts work away from its attention gate (layer-0 gate norm drops, L24: 3.75→2.08 aux3k), only at layer 0: ![aux attn gate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_attn_gate_profile.png)

**Final train loss — the aux is a small win at depth.** Final cross-entropy (last-30-step avg): the aux is slightly *better* than plain at L12/L18/L24 and a hair worse at L6.

| depth | plain | aux1k | aux3k |
|---|---|---|---|
| L6  | 2.065 | 2.069 | 2.069 |
| L12 | 1.910 | 1.904 | 1.902 |
| L18 | 1.800 | 1.790 | 1.789 |
| L24 | 1.748 | 1.743 | 1.742 |

So the gradient rebalancing comes with a small (−0.006 to −0.011) final-train-loss improvement at depth — modest, and aux3k ≈ aux1k. The raw eval/paloma numbers were inflated by an eval-time bug (loss called with `step=None` → aux applied at full weight at eval, +~0.1×first-layer-CE); fixed so eval reports pure CE (training was always correct).

**Net:** the aux durably rebalances the early blocks from attention-gating toward routed-expert compute — a real gradient/utilization effect that scales with depth and duration — but it did **not** move final loss at these settings.

## 5. AttnRes tuning — from marginal to a real win

The first AttnRes pass gave only ~0.01 macro loss. Investigating the optimizer routing revealed the per-layer pseudo-queries were being **MuonH-updated** (scan-stacking makes each `[num_layers, d]` query a 2D leaf, which the shape-based `create_mask` sent to MuonH). Fixing that — route queries to **Adam**, **zero-init** them (uniform depth-attention at init), a **parameter-free key norm** (the learnable gain is redundant with the query), and a **lower query LR** — turned AttnRes into a solid ~0.05 win. All d512, N=8, data-matched; Paloma macro loss (final), lower better.

**Tuning progression at L12 (each row adds one change):**

| # | config | Paloma | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | baseline (no AttnRes) | 2.963 | — |
| 1 | + AttnRes, query on **MuonH**, rand-init, learnable key-norm | 2.953 | −0.010 |
| 2 | query → **Adam** group (rand-init) | 2.951 | −0.012 |
| 3 | + **zero-init** query | 2.935 | −0.028 |
| 4 | + **param-free** key-norm (neutral, as predicted) | 2.935 | −0.028 |
| 5 | + query **LR 0.1×** | 2.916 | −0.047 |
| 6 | + query **LR 0.05×** (best) | 2.915 | **−0.048** |

Zero-init is the single biggest lever; the param-free key-norm is neutral (confirming the gain is absorbed by the query); the query LR wants to be ~0.05–0.1× the adam LR.

**Query-LR sweep** (config = zero-init query + param-free key-norm):

![AttnRes query-LR sweep](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attnres_qlr_sweep.png)

| query LR × | L6 Paloma | L12 Paloma |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline (no AttnRes) | 3.156 | 2.963 |
| 1.0 | 3.146 | 2.935 |
| 0.5 | 3.137 | 2.931 |
| 0.3 | 3.136 | 2.921 |
| **0.1** | **3.130** | 2.916 |
| **0.05** | 3.134 | **2.915** |
| 0.01 | 3.135 | 2.924 |

**Config ablation across depths** (final Paloma; "run" = still training):

| depth | baseline | MuonH-q | Adam-q rand | Adam-q **zero** | best (zero + pfkn + qlr) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| L6  | 3.156 | — | 3.156 | 3.145 | **3.130** (0.1×) |
| L12 | 2.963 | 2.953 | 2.951 | 2.935 | **2.915** (0.05×) |
| L18 | 2.860 | 2.855 | 2.854 | **2.820** | (qlr not run) |
| L24 | 2.787 | 2.775 | run | run | — |

Zero-init query alone is a large jump at depth (L18 −0.040 vs baseline; L12 −0.028). The query-LR sweep (L6/L12 only so far) adds another ~0.02. Deeper zero-init runs (L24) and L48 across configs are still training; qlr sweep at L18/L24 is the natural next step.

Plots + data under `experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/` (branch `depth-scaling-analysis`, commit `ec38f6fe30`). Feature commits on `fast-track-first-layer-aux`.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
At 12 Layers Block Attention Residuals is showing 2.915 macro loss vs 2.963 baseline (roughly 38% speedup), after tuning LR, init to zero, putting in Adam, and removing learnable portion of norms on residual keys. This is extremely good for just some light-weight query vectors.

Will be swapping to attention residuals and basing future depth studies around that.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Tuned AttnRes lifts the early-layer routed-expert gradient (d512, 12 layers)**

Per-layer routed-expert grad norm at the training midpoint (100-step avg, steps ~2335–2435 of 4770), for the best tuned config `ft-attnres-pfkn-qlr005-d512-L12` (zero-init query, parameter-free key-norm, query LR 0.05× → Paloma **2.915** vs baseline **2.963**) against the plain-residual baseline `ft-d512-L12-data2x`.

![tuned AttnRes routed grad by layer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/a5dac3837b63e37701aea942e22b353c1e38065d/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attnres_tuned_routed_grad_L12.png)

| layer | baseline | AttnRes tuned |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.0049 | **0.0134** (2.7×) |
| 1 | 0.0140 | **0.0214** (1.5×) |
| 2 | 0.0194 | 0.0177 |
| 3–8 | ~0.020–0.023 | ~0.017–0.024 (≈ equal) |
| 11 (last) | 0.0318 | 0.0282 |

The baseline routed-grad ramps steeply from a tiny layer-0 up to the late layers; tuned AttnRes **lifts layers 0–1** (layer 0 ~2.7×), merges with baseline by layer ~3, and is slightly lower at the deepest layer. So AttnRes gives the first-layer routed experts much more gradient — the same "save the lower-layer experts" behaviour as the first-layer aux loss — **but here it also improves loss** (−0.048 macro, ≈1.39× compute-efficient per the fast_track law), whereas the aux loss lifted the gradient without a loss win.

Routed = quadrature of `grad/norm/stacked_blocks.<i>.{mlp.*, mlp_gated_norm, rms_mlp, sconv_mlp}`. Data committed at `a5dac3837b` under `experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/`.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## Experiment: multi-latent MoE (per-expert latent projections)

### Initiating prompt (verbatim)

> ok now follow agent.md and lets try multi-latent moe. first to just get our bearings, take the baseline and move the latent projections into the routed experts, so each expert has their own latent projections. this means we need to pass the full activation to the target GPU. Still able a learnable rms-norm after the latent projection in, so each expert needs its own rms norm too. make sure these latent projections still route to Muon correctly.

### Idea

Baseline LatentMoE uses one **shared** `w_latent_down (d→lat)` + shared `latent_norm` + shared
`w_latent_up (lat→d)`, so all experts share a single latent subspace. This variant gives **each
expert its own** latent-down, learnable latent RMS-norm, and latent-up — each expert selects its own
subspace. The all-to-all then transports the **full d-dim** activation (≈`d/lat`× ≈2× more dispatch
bytes) instead of the compressed latent.

Motivation: our LatentMoE latent-compression runs showed a real quality penalty vs uncompressed
(recovered ~half by "more experts, not fatter"); a shared rank-`lat` bottleneck across all experts is
a prime suspect. Per-expert subspaces test whether that shared bottleneck is the cost.

### Implementation (behind `per_expert_latent`, default off → shared path byte-identical; hero-safe)

Branch: `multi-latent-moe` (off the baseline + PR#9287 budget fix). Edit points and the CPU/GPU
verification plan are in [`.agents/projects/multi-latent-moe.md`](../blob/multi-latent-moe/.agents/projects/multi-latent-moe.md):
model.py `MoEMLP`, `grug_moe.py` `MoEExpertMlp`/`moe_mlp`, `_moe/ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all.py`
`_compute_pooled` (+ CPU fallback), `optimizer.py` `create_mask`, `launch.py` flag.

Per-expert weights: `w_latent_down [E,d,lat]`, `latent_norm_gain [E,lat]`, `w_latent_up [E,lat,d]`.
Optimizer routing (explicit ask): the 3-D latent matrices → **muonh** (matrix catch-all, like
w_gate/up/down); the per-expert **norm gain** → **adam** (guarded by name so it doesn't hit the
ndim→muonh fallback).

### Result metric
`eval/paloma/macro_loss` (data-matched ladder), vs the baseline / shared-latent LatentMoE.

### Status
Design + plan + branch landed; implementation in progress behind the flag.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Result: per-expert latent projections give a small, consistent quality win but are net-negative in wall-clock (throughput cost dominates). Closing.**

Ran the "get our bearings" gate-1 comparison at d512 and d768 (data-matched), each expert with its own latent-down / learnable latent RMS-norm / latent-up (full d-dim dispatch in the all-to-all), vs the shared-latent LatentMoE control (`mlmoe-fsdp-base-*`).

| rung | shared latent (baseline) | per-expert latent | Δ Paloma | throughput | effective speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 3.152 (1.86M tok/s) | **3.141** (1.14M tok/s) | **−0.011** | 0.61× | **0.65** |
| d768 | 2.872 (1.00M tok/s) | **2.861** (0.58M tok/s) | **−0.011** | 0.58× | **0.62** |

Runs: baselines `mlmoe-fsdp-base-{d512,d768}`; variant `mlmoe-pe-latent-d512c` / `mlmoe-pe-latent-d768` (the d512/d512b attempts failed early; d512c is the valid d512 point). Effective speedup per `agent.md` (data-matched → tokens; `L=1.2+A·C^−0.0842`).

### Read
- **The shared rank-`lat` bottleneck is a real cost, but a small one** — giving each expert its own latent subspace improves Paloma macro loss by a consistent **−0.011** at both scales (≈1.07–1.08× compute-equivalent). So the hypothesis (shared bottleneck ⇒ quality penalty) is confirmed in direction, but the magnitude is modest.
- **The fix is too expensive to be worth it.** Per-expert projections force the all-to-all to transport the full d-dim activation instead of the compressed latent (~40% lower throughput at both rungs). The ~0.011 loss gain is nowhere near enough to offset that: **effective speedup ≈ 0.62–0.65 (net slower)**.

### Conclusion
Per-expert latent projections **do not pass** as a promotable change — a genuine but small quality gain, swamped by the dispatch-bandwidth cost. Not worth carrying to the d1024/d1280 gate. The `per_expert_latent` flag (branch `multi-latent-moe`) stays default-off / shared path byte-identical, so nothing is regressed. If the shared bottleneck is worth revisiting, a cheaper direction than full-d-dim dispatch (e.g. a small number of *shared* latent subspaces experts select among, keeping compressed transport) would be the follow-up. Closing as a completed (net-negative) experiment.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Loss change here is very minor, indicating direction isn't worth pursuing.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

Residual-stream (hidden_dim) scaling on the fast_track MLA + Inkling MoE stack, and the full architecture path that got there from the GQA baseline. All runs are **data-matched** (`--match data`) to the baseline token budget per rung, so the quality metric is an equal-data comparison. **Result metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss`** (lower is better).

**Final conclusion:** at these layer depths, **2× residual-stream scaling is ~neutral on FLOP compute-efficiency (0.99–1.03×) but a positive wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×) once MFU is accounted for** — the wider matmuls run at much higher utilization (MFU roughly doubles). 3× residual is a net-FLOP loss (0.84–0.92×) but still a wall-clock win (1.10–1.33×).

Branch: [`fast_track_mla_inkling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fast_track_mla_inkling) @ `7cffe00c3f`
Launcher: [`experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fast_track_mla_inkling/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py)

## Initiating prompt (verbatim)

> now lets add a variation where we scale the residual stream by 2x. then another where we scale it by 3x. for all of these, have the step count match the baseline, and have the LR match the baseline. Then do another 8 where we let the LR rescale with the new hidden_dim. flops should be relatively similar, since only a small portion of the flops are hidden_dim->kv, ->q, o->hidden_dim, and hidden_dim->latent, and hidden_dim->vocab. before kicking off these 8x2, list out the flops of these vs their baselines.

## Setup

- Ladder rungs d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280, one 8×H100 node each, `SEQ_LEN=4096`, tokenizer `hero-bpe-v16384` (vocab 16384), MoE `MOE_TPP=60` data budget.
- Data-matched steps per rung: 2413 / 7005 / 9366 / 16839 (tokens 1.27 / 3.67 / 9.82 / 17.66 B).
- "New baseline" stack = **MLA + Inkling rel-pos bias (RoPE dropped, 128-dim content-only heads) + output latent + no shared experts + top-12 routing + Q/O latent = hidden/2, KV latent = 512 + adam-routed bias weights.**
- Residual scaling = widen `hidden_dim` by N×, **all internal module dims pinned at baseline** (heads, MLA/MoE latents, intermediate); only the residual↔module boundary projections grow. Fan-in-correct init applied.

## Path from GQA → the new baseline (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GQA+RoPE baseline (`fasttrack-moe`) | 3.1559 | 2.8723 | 2.6330 | 2.5036 |
| GQA + Inkling bias | 3.1518 | 2.8593 | — | — |
| MLA + Inkling | 3.1384 | 2.8424 | 2.6104 | 2.4845 |
| MLA + Inkling + output-latent | 3.1448 | 2.8459 | 2.6183 | 2.4889 |
| MLA + olat + no-shared + top-12 | 3.1577 | 2.8571 | 2.6253 | 2.4985 |
| **new baseline (+ Q/O latent=hidden/2)** | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |

Takeaways: **MLA+Inkling beats GQA** (both RoPE and inkling baselines) and the gap widens with scale; dropping shared experts + top-12 + Q/O-latent compression is roughly loss-neutral vs plain MLA while buying inference/KV efficiency.

## Headline: residual-stream scaling (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| new baseline | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |
| residual ×2 | 3.1031 | 2.8173 | 2.5926 | 2.4699 |
| residual ×3 | 3.0851 | 2.8102 | 2.5846 | 2.4604 |
| **gain ×2** | **+0.056** | **+0.037** | **+0.032** | **+0.025** |
| **gain ×3** | **+0.074** | **+0.044** | **+0.040** | **+0.035** |

(LR-fixed vs LR-rescaled were interchangeable everywhere, ≤0.002 macro loss — shown: LR-rescaled.)

## FLOP efficiency vs MFU / wall-clock

Using the README MoE scaling law `L = 1.2 + 58.67·C^(−0.0842)` (L∞=1.2, α=0.0842): `baseline-needs` = compute multiple the baseline would need to match the residual's loss; `actual FLOPs` = the residual's per-token FLOP multiplier (= total, data-matched); `wall-clock` = data-eff × throughput ratio.

| rung / mult | loss gain | actual FLOPs | baseline-needs | **FLOP-eff** | tps ratio | **wall-clock** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 ×2 | +0.056 | 1.39× | 1.41× | **1.02×** | 0.91× | **1.28×** |
| d512 ×3 | +0.074 | 1.77× | 1.58× | 0.89× | 0.84× | 1.33× |
| d768 ×2 | +0.037 | 1.32× | 1.31× | **0.99×** | 0.92× | **1.20×** |
| d768 ×3 | +0.044 | 1.64× | 1.38× | 0.84× | 0.85× | 1.16× |
| d1024 ×2 | +0.032 | 1.27× | 1.31× | **1.03×** | 0.93× | **1.21×** |
| d1024 ×3 | +0.040 | 1.54× | 1.40× | 0.91× | 0.85× | 1.19× |
| d1280 ×2 | +0.025 | 1.25× | 1.26× | **1.01×** | 0.90× | **1.13×** |
| d1280 ×3 | +0.035 | 1.50× | 1.38× | 0.92× | 0.79× | 1.10× |

- **×2 is FLOP-break-even at every scale (0.99–1.03×)** — the residual-width params trade against compute at the compute-optimal frontier rate. Structural, not coincidence.
- **×2 is a wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×)** because the wider residual lifts MFU sharply (e.g. d768 baseline 7.2 → ×2 11.9 → ×3 17.1).
- **×3 is net-FLOP-negative (0.84–0.92×)** (diminishing loss gains vs linear FLOP growth) but still wall-clock-positive.
- Why ×2 is only neutral (not positive) on FLOPs: the Q/O/MoE latent ports are `hidden/2` (proportional), so widening the residual doubles both the useful state and the port cost. Fixing those ports to smaller *absolute* dims would drop the FLOP multiplier and turn ×2 into a net-FLOP win — untested follow-up.

## Scale (d1280, per-token / total)

| config | hidden | active params | lm_head | tokens | train FLOPs (incl lm_head) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1280 | 313M | 21M | 17.7B | 35.3e18 |
| residual ×2 | 2560 | 377M | 42M | 17.7B | 44.4e18 |
| residual ×3 | 3840 | 442M | 63M | 17.7B | 53.5e18 |

## Supporting ablations

- **QK-norm** (non-parametric RMS on per-head q/k): keep it. Removing it costs ~0.003–0.02 macro loss at every rung; `qk_mult=1` does not recover. Canonical MLA omits QK-norm, but it helps here.
- **LatentMoE compression (latent/4, flop-neutral)**: "more experts, not fatter." Spending the saved FLOPs on 2× experts (768 total / top-16) beats fattening the intermediate at both scales, recovering ~half the compression penalty:
  - d512: baseline 3.1559 · 2×-experts 3.1787 · fat-experts 3.1992
  - d768: baseline 2.8723 · 2×-experts 2.8902 · fat-experts 2.9091
- **Expert gate/up init sweep** (latent experts have fan-in=latent, not hidden): optimum at the fan-in-correct value, but only ~0.0025–0.005 macro loss — a correctness fix, not a lever.
- **LR treatment** (residual LR-fixed vs rescaled): indistinguishable (≤0.002).

## Excluded / caveats

- `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-d1280` is a **broken run** (loss rose vs its own d1024: 2.66 → 2.83) — excluded.
- GQA+Inkling only ran d512/d768. LatentMoE more-vs-fat and gate/up sweep only d512/d768.

## W&B runs (project `marin-community/marin_moe`)

Progression: `fasttrack-moe-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`, `ink-moe-{d512,d768}-re512d`, `ink-mla-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat512-{...}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat-nosh-k12-{...}`, `ink-mla-nosh-k12-qoh2-{...}`
Residual: `ink-mla-nb-resid{2,3}x-{lrfix,lrscale}-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`
Ablations: `ink-mla-nb-noqknorm[-qkm1]-{...}`, `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-{...}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-2xexp-{d512,d768b}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-gu{1p0,1p4,2p0,2p8,4p0}-{d512,d768}`

Run URL pattern: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/<run-name>`

comments.body:
The idea here was to make residual stream scaling extremely cheap (small vocab, latent projections on everything), then see if scaling it gave big boost to model quality for small change in flops. 2x scaling of the residual stream ends up being roughly flop neutral (maybe a slight boost if we retune its compute optimal ratio). The main gain here is on MFU. However the gains are not big enough to indicate its doing anything special. Basically, we just get gains proportional to the flops we spend.

What is looking reasonable is MLA + Inkling relative position bias + keeping QK-Norm (which is valid with MLA now, as seen in https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16310). Inkling relative position bias lets us have a clean 128 dim head.
